title: The Lorentz force: what a field does to a moving charge
subtitle: Steady fields; a point charge of either sign moving at nonrelativistic speed unless stated.
takeaway: Magnetic force is q v cross B: perpendicular to both v and B, so it turns motion and never changes speed or kinetic energy.

cards.title: The force law in words and symbols
items: The electric part pushes along E and does work; the magnetic part pushes perpendicular to the velocity and does none. Theta is the angle between v and B, so a charge moving parallel to B feels no magnetic force at all. The cross product fixes the direction: right hand along v, curl towards B, thumb gives v cross B, then apply the sign of q.
Split the motion into parts parallel and perpendicular to B before doing anything else; only the perpendicular part is turned.
Never use the left hand for negative charges. Compute v cross B first and apply the sign of q afterwards; otherwise the next positive ion gets the wrong arrow.

cards.title: Three properties worth memorising
items: Because the force is perpendicular to the velocity, a magnetic field changes the direction of motion but never the speed. Because the force is also perpendicular to B, a charge cannot be pushed along the field; motion along B is unaffected. A static B field can therefore do no work and cannot by itself speed a particle up.
These two perpendicularities are the whole chapter compressed: circles, helices, selectors and mirrors all follow from them.
Questions asking for the change in kinetic energy of a charge moving only in a magnetic field have answer zero. Electric fields do change energy; keep the two contributions separate.

cards.title: Work, energy and a signed charge
items: The magnetic force does no work at any instant, so the kinetic energy change of a charge in combined fields equals the electric work alone. For an electron moving against the electric field, the electric force is forward and it speeds up; the potential-energy bookkeeping carries the sign of q.
Work-energy answers must separate the two field contributions; otherwise a zero magnetic work term gets lost in an incorrect potential formula.
The magnetic force is not always zero when a particle is deflected; it is the work that is zero. Deflection and energy change are different questions.

cards.title: A feel for the tesla
items: One tesla exerts one newton on one coulomb moving at one metre per second. The Earth field is about 50 microtesla (half a gauss), a strong bar magnet about 1 T at its face, an MRI 1.5 to 3 T. Because the coulomb is enormous, the tesla is too; everyday laboratory fields are microtesla to tesla.
Large unit scales explain why magnetic forces on single static charges are hard to see yet forces on wire currents are ordinary.
Gauss and tesla mix-ups are common: 1 G = 1e-4 T. Convert before comparing with the Earth field.
The Earth field of 50 microtesla is 0.5 gauss; MRI runs 1.5 to 3 T, fifteen to thirty thousand gauss.

title: Circles and helices: the clock that ignores the speed
subtitle: Uniform B; v not parallel to B; nonrelativistic mass m.
takeaway: A charge perpendicular to uniform B circles with radius mv/qB and a period set only by q/m and B; speed changes the radius, never the time.

cards.title: The circle from the force
items: The magnetic force supplies exactly the centripetal force: |q|vB = mv²/r gives the radius. The period equals circumference over speed, so the speed cancels: a faster particle runs a proportionally larger circle in the same time. The cyclotron frequency omega_c depends only on the charge-to-mass ratio and the field.
This speed-independent period is the single most useful fact of the chapter: cyclotrons, mass spectrometers and magnetic resonance all rest on it.
Use the perpendicular component of velocity in r. Putting the full speed of a helix into the radius is the commonest error in trajectory problems.

cards.title: Sense of rotation and the charge sign
items: With B out of the page a positive charge moving right is pushed down and circles clockwise; a negative charge under the same motion circles anticlockwise. Either way the circulating charge is a tiny current loop whose own field at its centre opposes B: free-charge gyration is diamagnetic.
Get the direction from the cross product with a fixed convention; the sign of q flips the sense after the cross product is drawn.
Curl sense for electrons is not a separate left-hand rule; it is the same cross product with a minus sign applied last.
The circulating charge is a current loop whose own field opposes B: free-charge gyration is diamagnetic, the seed of diamagnetism in matter.

cards.title: The helix
items: An oblique entry separates into uniform motion along B and circular motion across it: a helix of radius r from v_perp and pitch = v_parallel times T. The circle lies in the plane perpendicular to B whatever the entry direction; the axis is along B. Theta is measured from B.
The two components never mix because each force component involves only the perpendicular velocity. Solving them separately avoids messy coupled equations.
Pitch uses v_parallel and T together; do not use the full speed in either factor. A charge moving exactly along B travels in a straight line.

cards.title: Numbers to anchor
items: An electron at 10^6 m/s in 1 mT has r = 5.7 mm and T = 36 ns, f = 28 MHz. A 10 MeV proton in 1 T: v about 4.4e7 m/s, r = 0.46 m, f = 15.2 MHz. Proton cyclotron frequency is 15.2 MHz per tesla, the number built into every cyclotron and MRI scanner.
Order-of-magnitude anchors catch unit slips: a computed electron gyroradius of metres in a modest field is wrong.
The proton spin precession frequency, 42.6 MHz per tesla, is a different constant from the orbital cyclotron frequency; resonance questions must say which one they mean.

title: Parallel and crossed fields: the velocity selector
subtitle: Uniform static E and B; crossed means perpendicular; v not relativistic.
takeaway: In crossed fields only particles with speed v = E/B pass undeflected, of either sign and any mass.

cards.title: The balance condition
items: With E along +y and B along +z, a charge moving along +x feels the electric force qE along y and the magnetic force -qvB along y: the two are antiparallel whatever the sign of q because both flip together. They cancel at v = E/B. Slower particles bend towards the electric force side, faster ones the other way.
The condition loses both q and m, so the selector hands downstream apparatus a single speed without caring what it filters.
The selector is for crossed fields only. If E has a component along B, the condition does not apply to that component.

cards.title: Why sign and mass drop out
items: Both forces are proportional to q, so equality never depends on the sign or size of the charge. Neither force contains m, so heavy and light particles are selected identically. This is exactly why the selector pairs with a mass spectrometer: the spectrometer then measures m/q from the radius of one known speed.
A clean experimental chain separates speed selection from mass analysis; combining them corrupts the inference.
For a beam of mixed species the selector transmits all with v = E/B; it does not purify charge or mass.
Real selectors correct for fringing at the ends; the balance v = E/B applies deep inside the crossed region only.

cards.title: Field along the motion
items: With E parallel to B the electric force accelerates along the field and the magnetic force only turns the perpendicular velocity. The result is a helix whose pitch grows or shrinks as v_parallel changes: a screw with a stretching thread. Radius is set by the (constant) perpendicular speed.
Parallel and crossed configurations must be recognised before computing; they ask different decompositions.
Do not apply v = E/B to a parallel configuration; there the charge simply accelerates and the speed is not constant.
With E parallel to B the perpendicular speed is constant and only the pitch changes; do not apply v = E/B to that geometry.

cards.title: Numbers
items: One hundred thousand volts per metre crossed with a tenth of a tesla selects one million metres per second. The region is usually a few centimetres long, so the transit time is tens of nanoseconds and stray fields at the entrance matter.
Checking the selected speed against the intended beam energy catches wiring or unit errors before the run.
Real selectors have fringing fields at their ends; the ideal balance applies deep inside the crossed region.
Over a 3 cm plate region a 10^6 m/s beam spends 30 ns inside; entrance fringe fields, not the formula, set the real resolution.
Transit times are tens of nanoseconds over centimetre plates.

title: The three-region method
subtitle: Field piecewise uniform in bounded regions; particle enters from outside.
takeaway: Mark the regions, draw an arc of radius r in each, and take the time from the angle turned, not from the full period.

cards.title: The protocol
items: In each uniform-field region the path is a circular arc centred on the perpendicular to v at the entry point, a distance r to the side the force points. Where the arc meets the boundary fixes the exit point; the tangent there is the exit direction; the angle varphi turned gives the time inside. Only a full circle takes one period.
Most exam trajectories are exactly this: geometry plus one radius formula. The perpendicular-at-entry construction fixes the centre without solving differential equations.
Fringing at a magnet edge breaks uniformity; if the field varies strongly over the orbit use the mirror picture instead.

cards.title: A strip of field
items: A particle entering perpendicular to a strip of width d crosses if r exceeds d, turning through arcsin(d/r) and leaving displaced sideways by r(1-cos varphi). If r is smaller it never reaches the far edge: it turns through 180 degrees and comes back out the entry face after exactly half a period, displaced by 2r. The borderline r = d is the minimum-speed question v_min = qBd/m.
The crossing condition and the return condition cover both exam families; check which regime the numbers give before computing angles.
The time in the strip is never the full period unless the particle closes a whole circle. For a half turn the time is exactly pi m/qB.

cards.title: A circular region
items: Entering a circular field region radially, symmetry makes the exit radial too: the arc centre, the entry point and the region centre form a right-angled figure with tan(varphi/2) = R/r. For r = R the deflection is a right angle. The result is geometry, not a new force law.
Radial entry is the special case that makes the deflection clean; off-radial entry needs the full three-step construction.
Radial exit is guaranteed only for radial entry. Do not impose the symmetry when the beam enters off-axis.
Radial entry into a circular region guarantees radial exit; off-radial entry breaks the symmetry and needs the full three-step construction.

cards.title: Worked numbers
items: Protons crossing a 5.0 cm strip: r exceeds d so they cross, turning 46 degrees in 28 ns (against a 219 ns full period) and displaced 2.1 cm sideways. Halve the speed and r halves to 3.48 cm: they turn back and exit 7.0 cm along the entry face after 109 ns, exactly half a period.
Same field, same particle, two regimes from one speed change: always compare r with d first.
A 46 degree deflection is not 46 degrees of a full circle in time: use t = varphi m/qB with varphi in radians.
Protons at 2 x 10^6 m/s in 0.30 T have r = 6.96 cm: crossing a 5 cm strip turns 46 degrees, halving the speed turns them back.
Same field, two regimes from one speed change: always compare r with d first.

title: The mass spectrometer
subtitle: Ions accelerated through known V; uniform B; semicircular entry perpendicular to B.
takeaway: Heavier ions land farther out: radius measures the square root of mass for fixed q, V and B.

cards.title: From acceleration to radius
items: Ions accelerated from rest through voltage V reach v = sqrt(2qV/m); the field then bends them into a circle whose radius carries both m and q. The detector sees the diameter 2r, so mass differences become distance differences: r is proportional to sqrt(m) at fixed q.
Eliminating the speed between the energy and radius equations leaves a purely measurable relation among V, B, r and m/q.
This r uses the speed from the accelerating voltage only if the ion started from rest and V is the total drop. Double acceleration needs the summed voltage.
The detector sees the diameter 2r, so the isotope spacing is twice the radius difference; never quote Delta r as the spot spacing.

cards.title: Isotope separation
items: Small mass differences halve in fractional radius, so resolution is limited by how narrowly the beam is defined, not by the formula. Singly charged uranium-235 and -238 at 10 kV in 0.50 T: radii 0.441 and 0.444 m, arriving 5.6 mm apart after their semicircles.
Half-relative-mass scaling is the working rule for estimating whether two isotopes resolve.
The separation at the detector is twice the radius difference, because each beam completes a half circle. Do not quote Delta r as the spot spacing.

cards.title: With a velocity selector
items: Bainbridge put a selector before the magnet: the ions then all have speed E/B1 regardless of how they were produced, and r is linear in m rather than its square root. The two instruments measure different things; combining them cleanly separates the variables.
Linearity in m simplifies calibration; the square-root form is for the pure acceleration design.
A selector narrows speed but transmits every mass at that speed; the second field is still needed to separate them.
Bainbridge linearises r in m by fixing the speed first; the pure-acceleration design gives the square root. Different instruments, different axes.

cards.title: Numbers and validity
items: Atomic mass unit 1.66e-27 kg; charge one elementary charge. The ions travel metres in modest vacuum; collisions with residual gas scatter the beam and set the practical resolution. Relativistic mass increase is negligible at 10 keV per nucleon.
Checking that Delta m/m is small validates the half-relative approximation before using it.
For molecular ions with different charge states, q must come from the ion source settings; equal m does not mean equal r.
For molecular ions read q from the ion source; equal m does not mean equal r when the charge states differ.

title: The cyclotron: a resonance machine
subtitle: Uniform B between two hollow dees; alternating gap voltage; nonrelativistic ions.
takeaway: Because the period ignores speed, a fixed-frequency gap voltage accelerates every turn until the ion leaves at the dee radius.

cards.title: Resonance condition
items: The ion coasts on semicircles inside the dees where the field acts and is kicked by qV0 each gap crossing. If the voltage has reversed in exactly one half period, every crossing adds energy. The spiral grows in radius, not in period. Final energy is set by B and dee radius R; a smaller V0 only means more turns.
Fixed frequency works only because T is speed-independent; that is the whole machine in one sentence.
Relativity breaks the fixed period by the factor gamma, which is why classical cyclotrons stop at tens of MeV for protons and never worked for electrons.

cards.title: Turns and timing
items: Each full revolution gains 2qV0. Protons in 1.5 T with R = 0.50 m reach 27 MeV: resonance 22.9 MHz, about 270 turns at 50 kV gap amplitude, 12 microseconds total flight, a path of roughly 250 m.
Turn count and total time are separate outputs; a high-voltage machine is compact in time but not in energy.
Energy per turn is 2qV0, not qV0: two gap crossings per revolution.
Total flight time is turns divided by frequency: microseconds of acceleration over hundreds of metres of spiral path.
Dee voltage fixes the turn count: 100 kV gaps give 135 turns for 27 MeV, so the spiral stays compact only while the frequency tracks the mass.

cards.title: Focusing and size
items: A perfectly uniform field lets ions drift out of the mid-plane; a field decreasing slightly with radius bends field lines and pushes strays back, the same physics as magnetic mirroring. Doubling the maximum energy needs four times the pole area at the same B. At 27 MeV the proton mass has already grown 3 per cent.
Scaling laws decide machine design before any detailed orbit calculation; pole area is the expensive part.
The size scaling is in B²R², so doubling B at fixed R quadruples the energy; quoting only V0 misses the physics entirely.

cards.title: Numbers check
items: Proton cyclotron frequency 15.2 MHz per tesla; electron 28.0 GHz per tesla. The maximum kinetic energy 27 MeV equals (eBR)²/2m with eBR = 1.2e-19 in SI. Comparing with m_p c² = 938 MeV gives the relativistic correction 2.9 per cent at that energy.
Anchoring the frequency per tesla and the energy formula catches most cyclotron exam slips.
Electrons are ultrarelativistic in any cyclotron-sized orbit; their machines are synchrotrons or linacs, not classical cyclotrons.
Alphas in a proton machine reach the same energy at half the frequency (q/m halves); verify by scaling before recomputing orbits.

title: Magnetic mirrors, bottles and adiabatic invariance
subtitle: Field varying slowly over one gyration; converging field lines; single particle.
takeaway: In a slowly converging field the quantity mv_perp²/2B is conserved, so a particle reflects where the field is strong enough.

cards.title: Why the force points to weaker field
items: Where field lines converge, divergence-free B gives a small radial component B_r = -(r/2) dB/dz. The azimuthal velocity crossed with B_r pushes along the axis towards weaker field, for either sign of charge because sense of gyration and sign flip together. The particle behaves as a dipole of moment mu in a gradient.
The gradient force is the magnetic analogue of the electric dipole gradient force; the same number mu is the circulating charge of the gyromagnetic section.
The push is towards weaker field for every charge sign. Reversing q reverses the gyration sense as well, not the net drift direction.

cards.title: The adiabatic invariant
items: Magnetic force does no work so total kinetic energy is fixed; as v_perp grows with B the parallel energy shrinks. Writing the perpendicular energy as mu B and tracking the exchange shows mu itself is constant when B changes little per orbit. Reflection happens where all energy is perpendicular: at B = B0/sin²(theta0).
An invariant replaces solving the orbit: it converts a trajectory problem into two energy statements.
Adiabatic invariance fails in sharply varying fields such as a pole edge; use the three-region construction there instead.

cards.title: Bottles and the loss cone
items: Between two mirrors a particle is trapped when its pitch angle is large enough that reflection comes before the throat. Particles inside the loss cone of half-angle theta_lc escape; for mirror ratio 10 the cone is 18 degrees. The Earth field is such a bottle: trapped particles bounce pole to pole, and those in the loss cone make the aurora.
Loss-cone physics is the same for fusion mirror machines and the Van Allen belts: different machines, one geometry.
Collisions scatter particles into the loss cone over time; a static bottle is never perfectly confining.

cards.title: Numbers
items: A 1 MeV proton mirroring in 31 microtesla has mu = K_perp/B of order 1e-13 A m² when perpendicular; the guiding-centre radius 37 km is tiny against planetary scales, which validates the averaging.
Separation of scales is what makes the invariant useful; check r_grad much less than B before applying it.
The invariant is of the motion averaged over one gyration, not of the instantaneous gyro-phase orbit.
A particle reflects where B = B0 / sin^2(theta0); at pitch 30 degrees it mirrors at 4 times the equatorial field.
A particle at 40 degrees pitch mirrors at B = B0 / 0.41 = 2.4 times the equatorial field. Check the trapping inequality before quoting the loss cone.

title: The Hall effect
subtitle: Flat conductor; steady current; uniform transverse B; carrier density n of one sign.
takeaway: The polarity of the Hall voltage reveals the sign of the carriers; the size counts them.

cards.title: The balance that makes the voltage
items: Carriers drifting along the current are pushed sideways by q v_d cross B and pile up on one edge until their transverse electric field balances the magnetic push. The steady Hall field is v_d B, and across the width w the voltage is IB/(nqt) with t the thickness along B.
Hall voltage is a transverse equilibrium, not an extra resistance; the field builds until the net transverse force vanishes.
Thickness is along B, width is across the voltage. Swapping them inserts the wrong dimension and can give voltages a factor of ten large.

cards.title: Carrier sign: one edge, two stories
items: Positive carriers drifting with the current and negative carriers drifting against it are both pushed to the same edge, because q v_d is the same vector either way. But positive carriers make that edge positive and electrons make it negative: the voltmeter polarity reads the sign. Zinc, cadmium and p-type semiconductors conduct by holes — this is how it was learned.
One geometric fact (same edge) plus one bookkeeping fact (edge sign) covers every Hall question.
Do not say electrons and holes go to opposite edges. Same edge, opposite voltage sign.

cards.title: What the magnitude measures
items: Combining Hall voltage with conductivity gives the mobility. Copper at 10 A in 1.0 T with n = 8.5e28 gives only 0.73 microvolts, while an n-type wafer with n = 1e21 at 10 mA in 0.50 T gives 0.31 V. The ratio is the carrier-density ratio: Hall sensors are semiconductors for exactly this reason.
Hall probes dominate magnetic sensing because low carrier density multiplies the signal.
Hall coefficient sign is 1/nq with q signed; a positive R_H means dominant positive carriers, not a positive charge density in metals.

cards.title: Geometry and numbers
items: Microvolt copper signals need lock-in amplification; volt-level semiconductor signals do not. Multi-band metals can show odd behaviour because both carrier types contribute; the simple formula assumes one type. Ordinary laboratory fields and currents give Hall voltages from microvolts to volts.
Keeping one carrier model explicit states the assumption; two-carrier Hall is the extension.
A reading of zero Hall voltage does not mean zero field: it can mean equal mixed carriers.
Copper gives 0.7 microvolts for 10 A in 2 T across 0.2 mm; a 0.1 mm semiconductor strip gives 40 mV for 20 mA in 0.5 T.

title: Drifts and the cycloid
subtitle: Crossed uniform E and B; or weak gradients with r grad B much less than B.
takeaway: In crossed fields the guiding centre drifts at E cross B over B squared, the same velocity for every charge and mass.

cards.title: Drift by force balance
items: A velocity perpendicular to both fields makes the net force vanish: q(E + v_d cross B) = 0 solves to v_d = E/B. No q and no m appear, so electrons and ions drift together, which is why the drift carries no current in a neutral plasma.
The E cross B drift is a motion of the whole guiding centre, not a charge-selective force.
Never call the drift a force. It is a velocity, and it is identical for opposite charges moving in opposite gyration senses.
The drift is a velocity of the guiding centre: no q and no m, so a plasma drifts as one and carries no net current.

cards.title: The cycloid from rest
items: In the drifting frame the particle simply circles at speed E/B; back in the lab that circle is carried along: a rolling-wheel cycloid with cusps if the particle started from rest. The arch height is 2r_c = 2mE/qB², the peak speed 2E/B, and the energy budget qE times height matches the peak kinetic energy exactly.
The drifting frame solves crossed-field orbits in one line; integrating the lab equations of motion reproduces the same curve.
The full speed at the arch top is 2E/B, twice the drift; energy checks must use the true speed, not v_d.
The cycloid is a circle of radius mE/qB^2 carried at E/B: arch height 2 r_c, peak speed 2E/B, energy gained qE times the height.

cards.title: Gradient and curvature drifts
items: Where B is stronger on one side, the orbit radius shrinks there and the guiding centre creeps sideways, perpendicular to both B and the gradient. The sign depends on the charge, so this drift separates charges and drives ring currents; the averaged force is -mu grad B, the same mirror force.
Gradient drift is charge-selective unlike E cross B drift; planetary ring currents and plasmas separate charge because of it.
Only the perpendicular velocity drifts; particles with parallel motion can also pick up curvature drift, a second comparable term.
Gradient drift reverses with the charge sign and drives ring currents; curvature drift needs the field line curvature, same order of magnitude.

cards.title: Numbers
items: An electron released from rest has r_c = 5.7 micrometres and rises 11 micrometres per arch; a proton on the same fields drifts at the same 10^5 m/s with a 1.0 cm gyroradius, 1836 times larger. Drift speeds are comparable to common plasma flows; gyroradii span micrometres to kilometres.
Comparing electron and ion scales separates the fast gyration from the slow common drift.
Proton and electron arch heights differ by the mass ratio even though the drift matches; do not transfer one orbit size to the other.
Electrons and protons in the same crossed fields drift together at 10^5 m/s but circle on radii differing by a factor of 1836.

title: Reading tracks: Thomson, momentum and detectors
subtitle: Nonrelativistic where stated; known E and B; deflections small unless solved exactly.
takeaway: Trajectories measure q/m or momentum: the 300 Br rule converts curvature to momentum at any speed.

cards.title: Thomson crossed fields
items: An electron beam first deflected by E alone then balanced by crossed B gives the classic e/m measurement: the electric deflection y over plates of length L at speed v = E/B eliminates v and leaves q/m = 2yE/(B²L²). Thomson measured it for cathode rays in 1897 and identified the electron.
This is the velocity selector used twice: once to know the speed, once to balance the deflection.
The formula assumes small deflection and the selector speed throughout; large angles need circular-orbit geometry.

cards.title: Momentum from curvature
items: A charged particle of momentum p in field B curves with radius r = p/qB. This holds at any speed when p is the relativistic momentum: chambers measure momentum, not energy. The 300 Br rule with r in metres and B in tesla gives MeV/c directly.
Detector physics is momentum physics; energy must be inferred with a mass hypothesis or a calorimeter.
Converting p to kinetic energy needs the right regime: p²/2m nonrelativistic, pc approximately ultrarelativistic, and something in between otherwise.
Chambers measure momentum, not energy; converting needs the regime: K = p^2/2m below, K about pc above.

cards.title: Bending magnets and spectrometers
items: In a bounded field region use the three-region method; in a thin lens approximation the impulse qBL over transit time gives the angular kick. Read a track by matching its curvature radius inside the field and the straight tangents outside.
Track reconstruction is the experimental form of the same circle geometry that exam strips ask for.
Multiple scattering and field inhomogeneity set real resolution; ideal radius formulas overstate precision.
A thin field region gives an angular kick qBL/p like a lens; inside the region use the arc, outside the straight tangents.

cards.title: Scales of detectors
items: A 1 GeV/c track in a 1 T field has radius 3.3 m — the scale of modern detector bores. Electron and positron tracks bend oppositely, allowing pair identification; neutral particles leave no track at all.
Knowing detector scales turns abstract formulas into estimates an examiner recognises as physically literate.
Curvature fits near the end of a low-momentum track can fail as the particle loses energy; use the momentum at the point of measurement.
1 GeV/c in 1 T curves at 3.3 m; electron and positron tracks bend oppositely, and neutral particles leave no track at all.

title: Biot-Savart: the source law
subtitle: Steady currents; vacuum; thin wires unless a density is specified.
takeaway: Every magnetic field of steady currents comes from the Biot-Savart integral; symmetry may replace the integration but never the physics.

cards.title: The law
items: Each current element contributes a field perpendicular to both the element and the line to the field point, falling as 1/r². The constant mu0/4pi belongs to Biot-Savart; a 2pi in a final answer comes from the geometry, not the constant. Direction from the cross product; magnitude with the sine of the angle between element and r.
Superposition of vector elements is the universal method: any geometry can be cut into elements even when no symmetry shortcut exists.
A straight segment whose line passes through the field point contributes nothing there — the cross product vanishes.

cards.title: From moving charge to wire
items: A point charge q moving at v makes a field proportional to v cross r-hat: the magnetic field of a moving charge is its electric field crossed with v over c². A wire is a parade of such charges; the current element I dl replaces q v. The identity B = v cross E over c² previews the relativistic origin of magnetism.
The factor 1/c² is why magnetic forces between ordinary charges are tiny compared with electric ones; wires are neutral so the electric part cancels and magnetism survives.
The moving-charge form assumes v much less than c; it is a quasi-static field, not radiation.

cards.title: Units and bookkeeping
items: Current elements I dl, surface currents K dA and volume currents J dV all enter the same integral. A rotating charged ring of charge Q at angular speed omega is a loop with I = Q omega / 2pi. Choose the substitution matching the dimensionality of the source.
One integral form covers wires, sheets and clouds; the measure is the only thing that changes.
Density factors are not optional corrections: a line current has no area density to multiply in later.
A rotating charged ring is a steady loop: I = Q omega / 2 pi. Match the current model to the actual charge motion.

cards.title: What the constant is not
items: mu0 over 4pi is the Biot-Savart constant; mu0 over 2pi is the infinite-wire answer; mu0 over 4pi times 2 is the semi-infinite end field. The magnetic and electric constants are tied by mu0 eps0 = 1/c²: magnetism is relativity applied to moving charge.
Separating the three familiar factors prevents the commonest constant mix-up in wire problems.
A formula quoting mu0/2pi is a finished wire result, never the starting constant.
mu0/4pi is the Biot-Savart constant, mu0/2pi the infinite-wire answer, mu0/4pi the semi-infinite end value: three factors, three situations.

title: Straight wires: finite by angles
subtitle: Thin straight conductor; field point perpendicular distance d from its line.
takeaway: A finite straight wire is integrated once by angles; the infinite answer is a limit of the same formula.

cards.title: Finite wire by end angles
items: For a wire segment, the perpendicular distance d to the field point and the end angles alpha, beta measured at the point between the perpendicular and the ends give the field magnitude mu0 I (sin alpha + sin beta)/4 pi d. Both sines are positive when the point is beside the segment and the perpendicular foot lies inside it.
The angle method collapses the Biot-Savart integral in one step; extending angles beyond the foot uses signed sines.
If the perpendicular foot falls outside the segment one sine enters with a minus sign. Blindly adding two positive sines doubles a contribution that should subtract.

cards.title: Limits
items: Both angles 90 degrees give the infinite wire, the classic mu0 I / 2 pi d. A semi-infinite wire with the field point level with its end has one angle 90 and one zero: half the infinite field. At the end of a wire the perpendicular foot is exactly at the end, the marginal case.
The three formulas differ by factors of two that come from geometry; recognising which applies is the exam skill.
mu0 I / 4 pi d is not the finite-wire formula evaluated carelessly; it is the specific end-on limit.
Semi-infinite at its end level: exactly half the infinite field. The end value is the marginal case of the angle formula.

cards.title: Compound wires add as vectors
items: A bent wire is a set of straight pieces; each piece contributes by its own angles and direction, and the fields add as vectors. Any straight piece whose line passes through P contributes exactly zero there. A square loop at its centre is four such pieces; the leads of a circular coil often vanish.
Superposition with the zero-contribution rule removes most of the algebra from compound figures.
A gap in a wire is not the same as the full wire minus nothing: model it as full plus a negative piece or as the two remaining segments.

cards.title: Numbers
items: Ten amps ten centimetres away makes a field comparable to the Earth: the reason lab wiring deflects compasses. A square of side a carries B = 2 sqrt(2) mu0 I / pi a at its centre; a regular n-gon approaches the loop answer mu0 I / 2R from below as n grows.
Comparing with the Earth field immediately tells whether a geometry is a serious magnetic disturbance.
Currents near compass measurements need magnetic hygiene: the wire field falls only as 1/d.
Ten amps at ten centimetres give 20 microtesla, comparable to the Earth: lab wiring visibly deflects compasses.

title: Loops and arcs
subtitle: Thin circular wire of radius R; field point at centre or on axis.
takeaway: A full loop gives mu0 I / 2R at its centre; an arc scales with its angle; the axis is one clean integral.

cards.title: Centre field and arcs
items: At the centre every element is perpendicular to its radius, so the integral is just the circumference: mu0 I / 2R. An arc of angle theta0 (radians) is that fraction of a loop: mu0 I theta0 / 4 pi R. Straight pieces whose lines pass through the centre contribute nothing.
Arc results follow from the loop by proportion; recompute nothing.
Theta0 must be in radians. A semicircle is pi, giving mu0 I / 4R, not 180 times anything.

cards.title: The axial field
items: Each element on the ring is at distance s = sqrt(R²+x²) from the point on the axis; the perpendicular components cancel by symmetry and the axial projections add with factor R/s. At x = 0 this is mu0 I / 2R; far away it falls as 1/x³, the dipole law of the next section.
The axial formula is exact on the axis and the bridge to dipole fields; off axis there is no elementary closed form.
Quoting mu0 I / 2R off the centre is wrong; the axis formula reduces to it only at x = 0.
Far off the axis the loop field is the dipole field of its moment mu = I pi R^2: the axial formula reduces to 2 mu0 mu / 4 pi x^3.

cards.title: The peak of the on-axis field
items: For a single loop the axial field is maximum at the centre and decreases both ways. Two coaxial loops can make a flat region where the second derivative vanishes — the Helmholtz construction of the extension section. Multiple turns multiply the field by N without changing the shape.
Field shape questions are calculus questions: study the derivatives of the axial formula, not just its value.
A maximum of B on axis is not automatically a point of zero gradient of the vector field; stability questions need the full components.
The single-loop axial field peaks at the centre; the Helmholtz pair cancels the second derivative to build a flat region.

cards.title: Turns, n-gons and compound loops
items: Multiple turns multiply every loop result by N: centre, axis and arc alike. A regular n-gon approaches the loop field as n grows; a square gives 2 sqrt(2) mu0 I / pi a and a hexagon sqrt(3) mu0 I / pi a at their centres.
The polygon family is a calibration ladder: each member checks the wire and loop formulas against each other.
Circumscribed polygon radius and side length differ; write R in terms of a before comparing with the loop limit.
Square: 2 sqrt(2) mu0 I / pi a; hexagon: sqrt(3) mu0 I / pi a; both climb toward mu0 I / 2R as the polygon grows.

title: Solenoid and toroid
subtitle: Long solenoid n turns per length; toroid with N total turns; steady current I.
takeaway: A long solenoid has uniform mu0 nI inside and zero outside; a toroid confines the field completely.

cards.title: Finite solenoid on axis
items: Stacking loop fields along the axis gives a simple result: the angles are subtended at the ends between the axis and the line to the point, both taken positive for an interior point, so the bracket is 2 deep in the middle of a long coil and 1 at an end. Interior of an infinite solenoid: mu0 nI; at an end exactly half; outside far away it leaks of order R/L.
The end factor one-half is a good exam trap and a useful check: the end sees only half the turns ahead of it.
The cosine convention must be stated: other texts measure both angles from one direction and subtract. Follow one convention through the whole problem.
The finite-solenoid cosine formula gives the interior plateau and the half value at the end from one expression.

cards.title: The toroid
items: The Amperian circle inside the winding encloses all N turns: B = mu0 N I / 2 pi r, falling as 1/r across the core. Outside the winding the enclosed current is zero and the field vanishes exactly. A toroid is the ideal closed magnetic circuit.
No leakage outside makes the toroid the clean demonstration of the loop law and the model for transformer cores.
Use total turns N for the toroid and turns per metre n for the solenoid; mixing them is a classic factor error.
Inside the toroid B = mu0 N I / 2 pi r falls as 1/r across the winding; in the hole and outside it is exactly zero.

cards.title: Ideal limits and reality
items: An infinite solenoid has perfectly uniform interior field and zero exterior field. A real one leaks at the ends and slightly outside the windings; the error is of order R/L. A solenoid of 1000 turns per metre at 1 A gives 1.26 mT, forty times the Earth field inside.
Knowing the size of leakage separates ideal formulas from apparatus statements.
For a short coil the infinite formula misleads badly; use the finite cosine form with the actual geometry.
Real solenoids leak of order R/L outside; the zero-outside statement is the infinite-length idealisation.
End field falls to half of the interior plateau; a finite solenoid leaks of order R / L outside. Quote the cosine formula at the ends.

cards.title: Field energy preview
items: A long solenoid of volume V stores (B squared over 2 mu0) times V, consistent with half L I squared with L = mu0 n squared times length. The preview is the working check for the induction module and gives the end force when two halves are pulled apart.
Energy density times volume is the fastest sanity check on any solenoid formula in a derived result.
Inductance per length assumes the infinite solenoid; a real coil has end corrections and stray field energy outside.
Field energy of mu0 n I at 1 T is 0.4 MJ per cubic metre wherever the field lives: the preview of B^2 / 2 mu0.

title: Magnetic moment and the dipole field
subtitle: Loop small compared with distance r; moment mu = NI A; uniform magnetisation cases noted.
takeaway: A current loop is a magnetic dipole: axial field twice equatorial, and the whole far field follows from mu = NI A.

cards.title: Defining the moment
items: The area vector follows the right-hand rule: fingers along the current, thumb along mu, which is also the direction of the loop field through its centre. For N turns multiply. A rotating charged ring of charge Q and angular speed omega has I = Q omega / 2pi and mu = Q omega R² / 2.
One vector fixes orientation, energy and torque; define it once and the dipole machinery runs.
Area is a vector by convention tied to the current sense; a clockwise loop viewed from the chosen side has mu the other way.
N turns multiply the moment; the right-hand rule around the current gives the normal, and the moment points along it.

cards.title: The far field
items: Far from a small loop the field is the electric dipole field pattern with p replaced by mu over eps0 c² bookkeeping: axial component twice the equatorial one at the same r, both falling as 1/r³. The full vector formula in components follows from the same expansion.
The factor two between axis and equator is the fingerprint of a dipole; every bar magnet far away obeys it.
Dipole formulas need r much larger than the loop size; at the loop centre use mu0 I / 2R instead.
On axis B = mu0 2 mu / 4 pi r^3 and at the equator half that: the same 1/r^3 law with two geometry factors.

cards.title: Magnets are current loops
items: A bar magnet, a solenoid end and a current loop are the same object at long range. Superposing two coaxial antiparallel loops of opposite circulation cancels their interior field and leaves only exterior dipole fields: the picture of a physical dipole with poles.
Identifying every magnet with a moment lets dipole formulas apply to atoms, coils and planets alike.
The pole model is a bookkeeping device; fields near the ends of real magnets are not inverse-square pole fields.
A bar magnet and a solenoid of the same moment are indistinguishable from outside; the pole picture fails inside the material.

cards.title: Numbers
items: A 100-turn coil of radius 5 cm at 1 A has mu = 0.79 A m². The Earth dipole is 8e22 A m². The Bohr magneton is 9.27e-24 A m² — atomic moments are twenty orders below laboratory coils, yet they are all that matter in materials.
Spending a minute on moment scales shows why magnetism is atomic physics plus relativity.
Moment of a magnet is independent of orientation but its torque is not; keep the vector and the scalar distinct.
A 2 A, 50-turn coil of radius 5 cm carries mu = 0.785 A m^2; the Earth torque on it in 50 microtesla is 39 micronewton metres.
The Earth torque on a small coil is mu B sin theta.

title: Ampere's law: when it works
subtitle: Steady currents; closed loop C; any surface bounded by C.
takeaway: The circulation of B equals mu0 times the enclosed current: always true, useful only where symmetry reduces the integral to B times length.

cards.title: The law and its proof sketch
items: Walking once around the infinite wire at radius r adds B times 2 pi r = mu0 I, independent of r: the 1/r of the field cancels the r of the path. Any loop that threads the wire once gives the same circulation; superposition makes the total circulation count enclosed currents.
The same cancellation built Gauss law with 1/r² and r²; here it is 1/r and r.
Zero circulation of a loop enclosing no current says nothing about the field along the loop: B can be large and tangential everywhere.
The law is exact for steady currents; the shortcut is the symmetry: without it the loop law is true and useless.

cards.title: Sign convention with a worked instance
items: Choose a loop direction; curl the right-hand fingers that way; the thumb is positive for threading currents. Wires of 5 A out and 3 A in threaded by an anticlockwise loop give enclosed 2 A and circulation 2.5 microtesla metres. The same loop reversed flips both signs.
A wrong direction choice flips both sides and preserves the physics; a wrong sign in copying does not.
The enclosed current is the net through any surface bounded by the loop, counting sign; two opposite currents can cancel.

cards.title: Honest usefulness
items: \text{useful iff }\mathbf B\parallel d\mathbf l\ \text{and }|B|\ \text{constant on segments}

The law is a constraint on an integral. It gives B only when symmetry guarantees the field is parallel to the path and constant along it, or perpendicular to some sides, or zero on them: infinite wire, long solenoid, toroid, thick cylinder, sheet. Finite solenoids and loops have no such symmetry; the law is true and silent.
Choosing between the loop law and Biot-Savart is choosing the method that the symmetry supports.
A symmetric-looking but finite source defeats the shortcut; integrate element by element instead.
Ampere on a finite solenoid or a loop gives nothing usable: Biot-Savart by angles and arcs is the honest route there.

cards.title: Two methods agree
items: The long solenoid can be stacked from loop fields or obtained from one rectangle of Ampère loop; the answers match exactly. Agreement of independent methods is the exam check that a derived formula is right.
Whenever possible solve a symmetric case both ways once; it calibrates every later shortcut.
Matching answers does not validate the method for the next geometry if its symmetry differs.
The solenoid both ways: stacking loops gives the cosine profile; the loop law gives the interior value in one line. They agree.
The loop law gives nothing for a finite solenoid; Biot-Savart by angles is the honest route. Symmetry is the deciding criterion.

title: Ampere applications: the eight fields
subtitle: High symmetry: wire, thick wire, cylinder, sheet, solenoid, toroid, coax, plate.
takeaway: Eight standard geometries cover most exam fields; learn the enclosed-current ledger for each.

cards.title: Wire family
items: Outside a long straight wire the answer is mu0 I / 2 pi r. Inside a thick wire of radius a with uniform current density, only the enclosed fraction counts: B grows linearly to mu0 I / 2 pi a at the surface. Two parallel wires with opposite currents between them add fields in the gap.
The enclosed fraction is the entire method: write I_enc(r) and divide by the path length.
Inside the wire the current is a fraction of I; multiplying the exterior formula by r/a twice gives the wrong power.
Inside a thick wire B grows linearly to mu0 I / 2 pi a at the surface; a shell carries all its current at the skin.

cards.title: Sheets and solenoids
items: An infinite sheet of surface current K has uniform field mu0 K / 2 on each side, opposite in direction, independent of distance. A solenoid wall is such a sheet wrapped up: interior mu0 nI, exterior zero. Two sheets of opposite K give mu0 K in the gap.
Sheet fields are the building blocks of the boundary-condition section and of overlap tricks.
The sheet formula has no distance because the sheet is infinite; a finite plate has edge fringing.
Between two opposed sheets the fields add to mu0 K; outside they cancel. The solenoid is this construction rolled up.

cards.title: Coax and hollow cylinders
items: For current distributed between radii b and c the enclosed current is the area fraction. A neutral coaxial cable with return current in the outer shell confines its field to the gap: inside the inner conductor and outside the cable the fields cancel exactly.
Coax is the exam case where the return current matters; write both contributions before canceling.
Ideal thin shells and uniform current densities are assumptions; surface currents change the face values but not the enclosed ledger.
Coax: zero inside the inner conductor and outside the cable; all the field lives in the gap annulus.

cards.title: The toroid and the decision
items: Use the loop law for infinite wires, long solenoids, toroids, thick cylinders and sheets. Use Biot-Savart for loops, arcs, finite wires, off-axis points and bent conductors. The decision table in the source chapter maps each geometry to one method.
A method decision made before algebra saves the exam; mixing methods mid-problem is where sign errors breed.
Compounding two symmetries (moving from wire to sheet) requires the new enclosed current, not a renamed old one.

title: Superposition tricks and no monopoles
subtitle: Linear media and vacuum; uniform current densities; steady fields.
takeaway: A hole is a full body plus a negative body; a gap is a full loop minus an arc; and no closed surface ever nets magnetic flux.

cards.title: Uniform fields from cylinders
items: A long cylinder of uniform current density J produces at internal offset r a field mu0 J cross r / 2. Two overlapping cylinders of opposite J leave a hole whose field is the difference: uniform, mu0 J cross d / 2, where d points from the removed centre to the full-body centre.
The overlap trick turns a hard geometry into two symmetric ones; the same method covers offset holes and missing arcs.
The uniform result is only in the overlap region where both bodies exist; outside it fields vary again.

cards.title: The gap in a loop
items: \mathbf B_{\rm gap}=\mathbf B_{\rm full}-\mathbf B_{\rm missing\ arc}

A circular loop missing an arc equals the complete loop minus that arc taken with opposite current. The full loop gives mu0 I / 2R at the centre; the missing arc by proportion. Compound and subtract with vector signs, never scalar magnitudes.
Negative-current bookkeeping is the magnetic twin of missing-charge superposition in electrostatics.
Field lines of pieces are not field lines of the sum; draw each contribution before combining.
A gapped loop is the full loop minus the missing arc taken with opposite current; compound with vector signs, never scalar magnitudes.
The overlap field is uniform and transverse to J. Moving the hole changes only d, never the field magnitude.

cards.title: No magnetic monopoles
items: Magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero: field lines that enter also leave. This is why there is no magnetic charge, no inverse-square magnetic Coulomb law, and why field lines close through magnets. It is exact, not an approximation of the current chapter.
Divergence-free B is the structural counterpart of Gauss law and the reason magnetic circuits are loops.
A point where B = 0 does not imply a magnetic charge absence test; only the closed-surface integral is identically zero.

cards.title: Field lines close
items: \text{outside N to S, inside S to N}

Bar magnet field lines run through the magnet itself, forming closed loops; cutting a magnet makes two smaller closed systems, never an isolated pole. Superconducting flux conservation and the absence of monopoles are the same statement in different language.
Closed field lines are why magnetic circuits are analogised to electric circuits with reluctance but no magnetic voltage source inside the gap.
Field-line maps drawn only outside a magnet invite pole thinking; draw the interior loop at least once.

title: Force on a current
subtitle: Uniform B on a straight segment, or local B along a curved path; steady I.
takeaway: The force on a wire is I L cross B; a curved wire in uniform field feels the force of its chord.

cards.title: From carriers to the wire
items: Each carrier feels q v_d cross B; a length L holds nAL carriers, so the total is nAL q v_d cross B = I L cross B since I = n q v_d A. The sign of the carriers is already inside the current direction: no extra sign remains to apply.
Deriving the wire force once from the carrier force shows where the Hall field enters and why the lattice feels the push.
For a negative carrier drifting opposite to conventional I the force is the same; do not flip the cross product.

cards.title: The chord theorem
items: In a uniform field the integral of dl along any path is the straight vector from start to end: a curved wire feels the force of its chord. A semicircle of radius R perpendicular to B feels 2IRB; a closed loop feels no net force at all in uniform B.
Chord reduction replaces path integration with two points; closed loops always cancel in uniform fields.
A closed loop can still turn; zero net force does not mean zero effect. Torque comes from non-collinear side forces.

cards.title: Numbers
items: I=10\ \mathrm A,\ L=0.5\ \mathrm m,\ B=0.2\ \mathrm T:\ F=1\ \mathrm N
One newton is the weight of 100 grams: motors stack many such lengths in strong fields. Force per metre of a 1 kA conductor in 1 T is 1 kN, which is why busbars are braced.
Newton-per-metre anchors keep design estimates honest in both directions of scale.
Sin theta in ILB sin theta is the angle between wire and field, not to the field normal; parallel wire to B feels nothing.
1 kA in 1 T feels 1 kN per metre: the structural design number for busbars and pulse-magnet windings.
Opposite currents 5 cm apart at 500 A press at 1 N per metre: substation busbars need bracing at every joint. Sin theta uses the angle between wire and field: perpendicular gives the full force.

cards.title: Non-uniform fields: the net force
items: A closed loop in a gradient feels a net force because the two sides see different fields. For an aligned moment the force pulls toward stronger field with magnitude mu times the gradient; anti-aligned reverses it. This is the electromagnet lifting a nail and the trap behind equal-and-opposite thinking.
The gradient force is the working principle of magnetic lifting and of mirror confinement; uniform-field results silently drop it.
Only the gradient along the moment orientation gives the simple mu dB/dx; transverse gradients produce sideways forces and torques.

title: Torque on a loop: energy and the galvanometer
subtitle: Small planar loop of moment mu in uniform B; torsion constant kappa for instruments.
takeaway: A loop in uniform B feels no net force but a torque mu cross B; its energy is -mu dot B and its small oscillations are the magnetometer.

cards.title: Couple and energy
items: Forces on opposite sides of a loop in uniform field are equal, opposite and displaced: a pure couple of magnitude mu B sin theta. The potential energy is lowest when mu aligns with B and highest anti-aligned; the force on the moment in a gradient is toward stronger field when aligned.
Torque and energy answer different questions: torque is the tendency to turn at fixed position; energy compares orientations and gives forces via gradients.
A loop at anti-alignment is in unstable equilibrium; torque vanishes there too, so zero torque does not imply the minimum.

cards.title: The oscillating magnet
items: A magnet swinging in the horizontal component B_H of the Earth field is a torsional pendulum for small angles: period set by moment of inertia I_m and the product mu B_H. Oscillation measures the product; deflection of a compass by the same magnet measures the ratio. Two measurements, two unknowns — the basis of absolute magnetic measurement.
Gauss method separates mu and B_H without any external calibration; this is why the old unit of B bore his name.
The period uses the horizontal component only; a magnet swinging near the dip poles has nothing to restore it.

cards.title: The galvanometer
items: A coil of N turns, area A in field B carrying current I twists a suspension of torsion constant kappa by angle proportional to I: the moving-coil galvanometer. Calibrated once, it reads current; paired with a known resistor it reads voltage.
The instrument is the torque law in hardware; its sensitivity is NAB/kappa.
Angle scales are linear only within the spring law; stop pins exist for a reason.
Current sensitivity of a moving-coil meter is NAB/kappa; adding a series resistor turns it into a voltmeter of range IR.

cards.title: Fixed current versus fixed flux
items: Virtual work on magnetic systems depends on the constraint. A current-driven circuit feeds energy from the source and the mechanical force follows the positive gradient of field energy; an isolated superconducting loop conserves flux and the sign flips. State the constraint before differentiating.
The two conventions are the commonest source of sign errors in force questions; the physics is identical, the bookkeeping is not.
Never mix the two rules in one problem; a battery-held coil and a persistent superconducting loop are different thermodynamic systems.

title: Forces between currents
subtitle: Long straight parallel wires; steady currents; vacuum between.
takeaway: Parallel currents attract and antiparallel repel: mu0 I1 I2 / 2 pi d per unit length, and the ampere is defined from it.

cards.title: The force law
items: Wire 2 sits in wire 1 field mu0 I1 / 2 pi d and feels I2 L cross B, giving the force per length. Same-direction currents attract; opposite directions repel. Each wire feels the other field only: a wire never pushes on itself.
Mutual force depends on the product of currents and falls as 1/d; the geometry is the same inverse-distance law as the field.
Adding the two fields at the midpoint before computing the force double-counts; each wire responds to the other field alone.
Wire 2 feels wire 1 field only; a wire never pushes on itself, whatever the current distribution inside it.

cards.title: The ampere, defined
items: The classical definition: one ampere is the current in each of two long parallel wires one metre apart giving two tenths of a micronewton per metre. Since 2019 the ampere is fixed by the elementary charge, but the force formula is unchanged.
The tiny force shows again that wire magnetism is weak per amp, yet measurable because currents can be large.
Post-2019 definitions change the unit bookkeeping, not Maxwell equations; never rewrite mu0 in the force formula.
Since 2019 the ampere is fixed by the elementary charge; the force formula is unchanged and still defines the practical scale.

cards.title: Newton third law
items: The pair forces are equal and opposite even though each wire feels only the other field. When currents change, the mechanical forces still balance but field momentum changes; the missing momentum is stored in B, not lost.
Third law holds for steady circuits as a statement about wires; the field carries momentum in time-dependent cases.
Do not add self-force: an element of wire is not pushed by its own field; the divergence of the wire model is an exam classic.
Steady circuits satisfy the third law as wire forces; during switching the field momentum changes and balances the books.

cards.title: Scaling
items: Doubling one current doubles the force; halving the distance doubles it. Two 1 kA busbars 10 cm apart press at 2 N per metre — structural bracing is standard. Pulse magnets see forces proportional to I² and can burst their windings.
I² scaling underlies both motor design and the pinch effect; one mental square catches many factor-of-two slips.
Currents induced during switching can repel or attract contrary to the steady-state expectation; watch the direction of each current at the instant considered.
Two 1 kA busbars 10 cm apart press at 2 N per metre; pulse forces scale as I squared and can burst windings.

title: Magnetic pressure and field energy
subtitle: Surface currents and field discontinuities; ideal sheets; uniform fields on each side.
takeaway: A field pushes on the currents that confine it with pressure B squared over 2 mu0; a solenoid wears its own field like a pressure vessel.

cards.title: Force on a current sheet
items: A sheet with surface current K separates fields B1 and B2. The sheet feels only the field of the rest, the average of the two sides; with B1 - B2 = mu0 K the force becomes the difference of squares over 2 mu0. At 1 T this is four atmospheres on the windings.
The factor one-half is the conductor-stress factor again: a current sheet cannot push on its own field.
The direction is from strong field to weak regardless of current direction; the squares erase the sign.

cards.title: Solenoid end force and energy density
items: Cut a long solenoid and the halves attract with pressure times area: field lines behave as if under tension along themselves and pressure across. A 1 T solenoid of 10 cm² bore pulls together with 400 N. The same B²/2 mu0 is the energy density: 0.4 MJ per cubic metre at 1 T.
Energy methods give the end force without integration: separating halves by dx creates field volume A dx at energy density B²/2 mu0.
The energy argument assumes constant current maintained by a source; at fixed flux the sign of the virtual-work rule flips.
B^2 / 2 mu0 is both the pressure on the windings and the energy density: 4 atmospheres and 0.4 MJ per cubic metre at 1 T.

cards.title: Boundary conditions
items: Across any surface current the tangential B jumps by mu0 K and the normal component is continuous. The solenoid field steps from mu0 nI to zero exactly at the winding sheet K = nI. A perfect diamagnet with B = 0 inside feels the full B²/2 mu0 from outside.
Boundary conditions are the local form of the loop and pillbox arguments; use them to fix field values at surfaces.
Outside an ideal long solenoid the field is zero, so the hoop stress is inside-to-out; a finite solenoid leaks and reduces the ideal stress a little.
Across a surface current the tangential B jumps by mu0 K and the normal component stays continuous: the local form of the loop argument.

cards.title: Numbers and the motor puzzle
items: At 10 T the pressure is 400 atmospheres: high-field magnets are built like pressure vessels. A running motor still has back-EMF accounting; the magnetic forces transmit mechanical power while B itself does no work on charges — the energy comes from the source through the electric field the source maintains.
Pressure scales as B², so doubling field quadruples stress: the practical limit of pulsed and superconducting magnets.
A quenching MRI magnet dumps megajoules of field energy into heating; B²/2 mu0 is real stored energy, not a fiction of the formula.

title: Rotating charges: the gyromagnetic ratio
subtitle: Rigid bodies whose charge is distributed like their mass; nonrelativistic rotation.
takeaway: Any such rotating charged body has mu/L = Q/2m: the same ratio for ring, disc or sphere.

cards.title: Ring to body
items: A spinning charged ring is a current Q omega / 2pi with moment mu = Q omega R squared over 2 and angular momentum L = m R squared omega; the radius cancels in the ratio. A stack of rings with the same charge-to-mass ratio keeps the same mu/L. The gyromagnetic ratio is a property of Q/m alone.
Universality of Q/2m lets one check any rotating-charge geometry against one ratio.
The ratio is classical; electron spin has g = 2 and is not a spinning ball. Quote the anomaly, do not hide it.
For charge distributed like mass the gyromagnetic ratio is q/2m; the electron spin value is twice it, a quantum fact.

cards.title: The Bohr magneton
items: For an electron on an orbit of angular momentum hbar the moment is one Bohr magneton, the natural unit of atomic moments. Paramagnetic salts are measured in mu_B per atom; the Curie law uses the same unit.
Atomic magnetism is measured in moments that are tiny per atom but enormous per mole.
Spin moment is close to mu_B while spin angular momentum is hbar/2: the factor two is the famous g = 2.
The Bohr magneton is the natural unit of atomic moments; paramagnetism is measured in multiples of it.
Spin g-factor is twice the orbital value. The nuclear magneton is smaller by the proton-to-electron mass ratio.

cards.title: Rotating disc and shell
items: A rotating charged disc is stacked rings: each ring of width dr contributes mu0 dI / 2r = mu0 sigma omega dr / 2 at the centre, the same for every ring, giving mu0 sigma omega R / 2. A rotating uniformly charged shell gives a uniform interior field two-thirds mu0 sigma omega R, the same surface current as the magnetised sphere.
Ring stacking is the first real use of the solenoid logic; the shell case previews magnetisation in matter.
The disc centre field grows with R at fixed sigma and omega; that is not an approximation error but more current at larger radii.

cards.title: Numbers
items: A macroscopic spinning charge is a feeble magnet: its centre field 0.6 nT is a hundred-thousandth of the Earth. At atomic scales the same physics with hbar-sized angular momentum gives mu_B, perfectly measurable in a lab balance of moments.
Contrasting human and atomic scales explains why magnetism is an atomic phenomenon despite being discovered in lodestones.
Charged macroscopic rotors radiate and lose energy; the static formulas assume steady maintained currents.
A ring of 2 microcoulombs at 50 rev/s on a 5 cm radius: I = 100 microamp, mu = 7.85e-7 A m^2, and mu/L = Q/2m exactly.

title: The magnet as a current distribution
subtitle: Uniform magnetisation M; linear response only where stated; ellipsoids for demagnetising factors.
takeaway: Uniform M makes only surface bound current K_b = M cross n; a magnetised cylinder is literally a solenoid with nI = M.

cards.title: Bound currents from M
items: A slab magnetised along its normal is a stack of current loops: interiors cancel, the rim does not. Matching the slab moment MAt to a rim loop gives current M per unit height, K_b = M cross n. Where M varies, a volume current curl M remains.
Every magnetostatics problem in matter becomes a free-current problem once bound currents replace the material.
Bound surface current direction follows the right-hand rule with M and the outward normal; flipping the normal flips K.

cards.title: The magnetised sphere
items: A uniformly magnetised sphere has K_b = M sin theta, the same as a rotating charged shell: uniform interior field two-thirds mu0 M and a pure dipole outside with moment M times volume. A long cylinder instead has B = mu0 M inside - larger because its demagnetising field is smaller.
Demagnetising factors depend on shape: sphere one third, long cylinder zero, thin plate one. Shape decides the internal field for the same M.
The interior sphere field is uniform despite the varying surface current; do not expect a solenoid-like axial falloff inside a sphere.

cards.title: Cutting and poles
items: Cutting a bar magnet creates two complete magnets, each with its own current distribution and closed field lines. The pole picture is bookkeeping: north and south are never separated because field lines close through the material.
Bound-current language never invites monopoles; pole language always does. Prefer currents for derivations.
Demagnetising fields of short bar magnets are strong: a short fat magnet magnetises itself less than a long thin one of the same M.
Cutting a magnet makes two complete dipole systems; the poles are bookkeeping, not particles, and no bound pole charge exists.

cards.title: The slab moment ledger
items: A slab of thickness t magnetised along its normal has total moment M A t equal to a single rim loop of current I_b around the edge: I_b = M t, a current M per unit height. Two half-thick slabs stacked give the same total rim current as one full slab.
The ledger is the cleanest derivation of bound surface current and rehearses the solenoid identity n I = M.
The rim current is bound current: no free charge moves and no wires are attached. Confusing it with conduction current breaks the H definition.
The moment ledger: mu = M V with V the volume; a 1 cm sphere at M = 10^6 A/m carries 4.19 A m^2 and matches its exterior dipole exactly.

title: B, H and M inside matter
subtitle: Linear media M = chi H where stated; ferromagnets use loops, not constants.
takeaway: H counts free currents only; B is the real field. In a long solenoid H = nI and B = mu_r mu0 nI.

cards.title: The auxiliary field
items: \mathbf H=\frac{\mathbf B}{\mu_0}-\mathbf M,\qquad \oint\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf l=I_{\rm free}

Ampères law with all currents is awkward because bound currents depend on the material response. Solving for the free-current circulation defines H: its loop integral counts free current only. B remains the force-giving field; H is a bookkeeping convenience.
Using H makes magnetic circuits and solenoid problems independent of the material magnetisation details.
H is measured in A/m and B in tesla. Numerically similar-looking values in gauss and oersteds come from mixed unit systems; keep SI.
H is the field the free currents make; M is the material response; B is what drives charges.

cards.title: Linear media
items: For linear isotropic media M follows H with susceptibility chi, and B = (1+chi) mu0 H = mu_r mu0 H. In a long solenoid filled with such material H = nI stays fixed and B multiplies by mu_r. Diamagnets have tiny negative chi, paramagnets tiny positive; iron is neither linear nor constant.
The pair (H fixed by free current, B amplified by material) is the whole of linear magnetic circuits.
mu_r is not a constant for iron: it is a slope on the hysteresis loop and collapses at saturation. Quoting one mu_r for iron is an approximation at a stated operating point.

cards.title: Units and magnitudes
items: A 1000 turns per metre solenoid at 1 A has H = 1000 A/m and B = 1.26 mT in vacuum. Water chi about -9e-6, aluminium about 2e-5, iron can reach mu_r of thousands below saturation. Beware oersted-era confusion: 1 A/m corresponds to 4 pi times 1e-7 T in vacuum.
Practical susceptibility values span ten orders; knowing which side of unity a material sits on prevents order-of-magnitude disasters.
Do not insert mu_r into mu0 itself; write B = mu_r mu0 H as a product at the end.
H is measured in A/m: a 1000 turn/m solenoid at 0.5 A gives H = 500 A/m and B = 0.63 mT in air.

cards.title: The gapped circuit
items: A magnetic circuit of iron length ell with gap g under N ampere-turns has flux set by total reluctance: gap g dominates when mu_r is large. This is how transformer cores and electromagnets are designed: reluctance adds like resistance and the gap controls B.
Reluctance thinking turns field design into a circuit problem; mu0 NI plays the role of EMF.
If the gap is wide the flux fringes out of the pole area and the simple formula overestimates B; if iron saturates the formula fails differently.
Gapped cores: B = mu0 N I / (g + l/mu_r); the air gap dominates once g exceeds l/mu_r, which is how real chokes are designed.

title: Dia- and paramagnetism
subtitle: Closed shells for diamagnetism; independent moments for paramagnetism; weak fields where linearised.
takeaway: Diamagnetism opposes any applied field and is temperature-independent; paramagnetism aligns existing moments and follows Curie law.

cards.title: Larmor diamagnetism
items: An applied field changes orbital speeds so as to oppose itself: one sense of orbit slows, the other speeds up, both reducing the net moment along B. Averaging over orientations gives chi = -mu0 n Z e squared <r squared> / 6 m_e, tiny and negative, independent of temperature.
Diamagnetism is universal: every material has it; it is visible only where permanent moments are absent.
The classical electron orbit model gives the right magnitude but quantum mechanics is the real story; the sign and scaling are what the exam needs.

cards.title: Curie paramagnetism
items: Independent atomic moments of size mu align against thermal agitation: magnetisation is the Brillouin-tanh of x = mu B / kT, and for weak fields linear: Curie law chi = C/T. At room temperature a Bohr magneton in 1 T gives x of order 1/300 - weak alignment.
Curie law is a thermometer as much as a magnetisation law: measuring chi versus T extracts the moment per atom.
Curie law holds for independent moments only. Interacting moments make Curie-Weiss, and locked moments make ferromagnets.
Paramagnetism is alignment against disorder: Curie law at low field, saturation when mu B exceeds k_B T.

cards.title: Numbers
items: Water -9e-6, copper -1e-5, bismuth -1.7e-4, pyrolytic graphite up to -4e-4 across planes. A paramagnetic salt at 1 K in 1 T can reach substantial M because x = mu B / kT grows as T falls.
Order-of-magnitude tables are the fastest exam check on a computed susceptibility.
Superconductors are the exception with chi = -1, a perfect diamagnet; their levitation is not explicable by the Larmor formula.
Water chi about -9e-6, aluminium +2e-5, iron huge; at 1 K and 1 T the paramagnetic argument x = mu B/k_B T reaches 0.67.

cards.title: Adiabatic demagnetisation
items: Since M depends on B/T only, an isentropic field reduction from Bi to Bf scales the temperature the same way: a salt at 1 K in 1 T demagnetised to 0.01 T reaches 10 mK. The same magnetocaloric effect drives magnetic refrigerators near gadolinium Curie point.
The one-line scaling is an exam favourite: ideal paramagnet plus adiabatic gives direct temperature ratio.
Internal field and interactions set a floor; the ideal ratio fails at millikelvin and near ordering transitions.
Adiabatic demagnetisation: order paramagnets at high field and low T, remove the field adiabatically, and the spin temperature falls with the entropy.
Adiabatic demagnetisation reaches millikelvin from a 1 K start.

title: Ferromagnetism and hysteresis
subtitle: Exchange-coupled moments; domain structure; loop area is loss, not theory noise.
takeaway: Iron locks moments with exchange, not dipole coupling; its hysteresis loop is both memory and energy loss.

cards.title: Exchange, not dipole coupling
items: Two Bohr magnetons a quarter nanometre apart interact magnetically with only 5.5e-25 J, equivalent to 0.04 K: dipole forces cannot order iron at room temperature. Exchange energy J from Coulomb plus Pauli exclusion with z neighbours gives Tc of the right thousand-kelvin order.
The estimate that rules out the wrong mechanism is worth more than a memorised Curie temperature.
Exchange is quantum mechanical and has no classical dipole derivation; quote it as the mechanism and estimate its size.

cards.title: Domains and hysteresis
items: Domains are regions of aligned moments; walls move and moments rotate under H. Trained material follows a loop: B lags H, remanence is what stays when H returns to zero, coercivity is what must be reversed to erase it. The loop area in the (H,B) plane equals energy lost per unit volume per cycle.
Hysteresis is thermodynamics with a picture: source work minus stored energy is heat in the walls.
Soft and hard materials are not weak and strong magnets; they are narrow and wide loops - transformers u

cards.title: Numbers
items: Silicon steel loses about 1 J per kilogram per cycle; a 20 kg core at 50 Hz with 150 J/m³ loop area dissipates 20 W. Iron saturates near 2.1 T: no circuit formula can deliver more. Curie-Weiss chi = C/(T-Tc) describes the approach from the paramagnetic side.
Loop area times frequency times volume is the engineering loss formula every transformer question uses.
Above Tc the domains vanish; applying Curie law below Tc inverts the actual physics.
Silicon steel at 1.2 T and 50 Hz loses about 1.5 W/kg; a 20 kg core at 60 Hz dissipates roughly 20 W of hysteresis heat.

cards.title: Soft versus hard
items: Transformer cores want narrow loops and laminations to cut eddy losses; permanent magnets want wide loops so demagnetising fields do not erase them. A hard material in a core wastes its loop area as heat every cycle.
Choosing a magnetic material is choosing a loop shape for a duty, not choosing a bigger mu_r.
Laminations interrupt eddy currents whose loss scales as thickness squared; solid cores run hot at power frequency.
Soft for transformer cores and shields, hard for permanent magnets; above the Curie temperature a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic abruptly.

title: Materials in circuits: cores, shields and forces
subtitle: Linear approximations below saturation; gap-dominated reluctance; soft iron for channelling.
takeaway: Iron channels flux like a wire channels current; the gap sets B; and field gradients pull iron towards stronger field.

cards.title: Cores and shielding
items: An iron core multiplies the solenoid field at the same free current; a closed iron shell shields its interior by guiding flux around it. The same construction builds electromagnets, transformer cores and magnetic screens. Saturation at 2.1 T caps the multiplication.
Magnetic circuits obey a reluctance version of Ohm law: ampere-turns drive flux through total reluctance.
Shielding works only for the field components the flux path intercepts; uniform static fields are hard to cancel with partial shells.

cards.title: Forces on materials
items: A magnetisable body in a gradient is pulled toward stronger field, roughly with stress B²/2 mu0 over the pole area: the paperclip jump. A superconducting plate supports the same stress in repulsion; a 2 kg magnet over 4 cm² needs 0.35 T at the plate.
Force from energy density in the gap is one line and agrees with virtual work at fixed current.
Saturation caps iron force: once M cannot grow, B in the gap stops scaling and levitation saturates.
Induced dipoles are attracted to field maxima either way; diamagnets and superconductors are pushed toward weaker field.

cards.title: The gapped electromagnet
items: The gap dominates when mu_r is large: B is set almost entirely by ampere-turns over gap width. Fringing adds effective gap; saturation subtracts effective mu_r. Design means deciding which limit the magnet sits in.
Reluctance in series is the design equation of motors, speakers and MRI yokes.
Never leave the gap out of a magnetic circuit calculation; iron reluctance is usually negligible, gap reluctance is not.
The gapped electromagnet: mu0 N I over gap plus reluctance of the iron path; fringe fields at wide gaps steal flux from the pole face.

cards.title: Saturation caps every circuit
items: Once iron saturates, mu_r collapses toward unity and extra ampere-turns buy almost no flux: the gapped formula fails upward. Electromagnet lifting force stops growing with current and transformer cores distort waveforms. Design means staying below the knee of the B(H) curve with margin.
Saturation is the engineering limit behind every magnetic circuit number; the linear formulas are local, not global.
Heating raises losses and shifts the knee; pulsed magnets may exploit deep saturation briefly but cannot hold it.

title: The Earth as a dipole
subtitle: Central tilted dipole plus stated local anomalies; slow secular variation.
takeaway: Declination, dip and the two components describe a station; tan(dip) = 2 tan(latitude) is the dipole identity.

cards.title: The three angles
items: Declination is compass deviation from true north, east or west; dip is the tilt of a freely pivoted needle below the horizontal. The horizontal component is what compasses and tangent galvanometers use; total field across India runs 25 to 65 microtesla. The magnetic pole near geographic north is a south pole of the dipole.
Angles and components answer different instruments; read the instrument, then take the matching component.
Dip is not declination, and the magnetic pole near the Arctic is not a north pole of the dipole.

cards.title: Dipole geometry
items: At magnetic latitude lambda the radial component is 2 cos-like and the tangential one sine-like in the dipole field, so the dip angle satisfies tan(dip) = 2 tan(lambda). Field strength grows from equator to pole as sqrt(1+3 sin²lambda) times the equatorial value.
One identity links a station dip to its latitude and checks internal consistency of field tables.
Local crustal anomalies shift both angles; the dipole relation is a model, and departures are real data.

cards.title: Measuring B_H
items: A tangent galvanometer in the magnetic meridian deflects a compass by theta with B_coil = B_H tan theta. A swinging magnet gives the product mu B_H; a deflected compass gives the ratio mu / B_H. Together they give both unknowns - Gauss absolute method.
Absolute magnetic measurement needs no external magnet reference: geometry, mass and time suffice.
Coil must lie in the magnetic meridian; misalignment measures a component and biases theta.
Tangent galvanometer: B_coil = B_H tan theta; oscillation gives mu B_H. Both measure the horizontal component alone.

cards.title: Earth and core numbers
