items: Equatorial surface field about 30 microtesla gives the dipole moment from mu = B_eq R cubed over 1e-7 in SI. A core-sized loop of radius 3.5e6 m would need two billion amperes: liquid-iron convection in a dynamo, decaying in a few 10^4 years if not maintained.
A one-line estimate shows why the field needs a dynamo and has persisted for aeons.
The dipole tilts about 11 degrees from the rotation axis and wanders; the geomagnetic poles are not fixed points.
B about 25 to 65 microtesla over the globe; the dipole moment 8e22 A m^2 needs a core current of about 2 GA to sustain it.

title: Flux: definition, sign and the changing bookkeeping
subtitle: Flat loop or coil; uniform B or a known profile; normal chosen once and kept.
takeaway: Flux is a scalar with a sign; choose the normal once, keep it, and the sign of every EMF follows.

cards.title: The flux integral
items: For a uniform field through a flat loop of area A the flux is BA cos theta with theta between B and the chosen normal: full BA face-on, zero edge-on, negative when the field crosses against the normal. A coil of N turns links N times the flux of one turn; the weber is one tesla square metre, and one weber per second is one volt.
The surface is any surface bounded by the loop; no-monopoles guarantees they all give the same answer.
Reversing the normal reverses Phi and every EMF computed from it. Fix the normal with the right-hand rule on the first line of the solution and never revisit it.

cards.title: Non-uniform fields
items: A rectangle a by b with its near side at distance d from a long straight wire: integrate mu0 I a dr / 2 pi r across the strip. The logarithm is the flux of the wire through the loop and simultaneously the mutual inductance of a wire and a loop per unit current.
One integral, two readings: flux now, mutual inductance later. Keep the geometry exact and the later sections inherit it.
The integral runs across the loop width b, not along it; swapping a and b silently changes the answer.
At d = 1 cm, b = 5 cm, a = 10 cm and 10 A the flux is 3.2 micro-weber: millimetre geometry makes microweber flux.

cards.title: Faraday and the charge that flows
items: An induced EMF appears whenever the flux through the circuit changes and never while it is steady, however large. The EMF is work per unit charge around the loop; in a resistance R it drives i = E/R, and the total charge passed during a flux change is Delta Phi over R, independent of how fast the change happened.
Charge depends only on the flux change; rate affects current and power but not the integrated charge: the flip-coil and the ballistic galvanometer.
Steady flux means no EMF even at tesla levels; only the derivative counts. And q = Delta Phi / R needs the circuit resistance R, not the load alone.

cards.title: The sign protocol
items: Choose the positive direction round the loop; let the right hand give the normal; compute Phi with that normal and its sign; compute dPhi/dt with its sign; then E = -dPhi/dt decides the current direction. The final Lenz check: the induced current opposes the change of flux. Worked drill: field into the page grows 0.2 to 0.6 T in 2 s with clockwise positive gives E negative, so the current runs anticlockwise, making outward flux against the growth.
Every sign error in the chapter is a skipped step; the protocol is Lenz law made mechanical and it exits with an independent check.
Do not flip the normal halfway through to make a sign come out; recompute instead. If the Lenz check fails, the error is in step three or four.

title: Faraday experiments and the loop rule
subtitle: Circuits of known resistance; flux changes by motion, rotation, deformation or switching.
takeaway: A current appears only while the flux changes; the four experiments differ in mechanism and agree in law.

cards.title: The four experiments
items: A magnet moved into a coil deflects a galvanometer one way; moved out, the other way; a second coil switched on gives a single flick; a loop rotated in a steady field gives a sinusoid. Same law, four mechanisms: motion of the source, motion of the circuit, switching, rotation. None produces EMF while the flux is constant.
Recognising which of the four a problem is decides what to differentiate: a position, a current, or an angle.
The flick on switching lasts only while the current builds; after the transient the flux is steady and the meter returns to zero.
The induced current direction always opposes the change: growth is opposed, decay is supported. Say opposes the change, not opposes the field.

cards.title: The charge protocol
items: Integrate the current over the change: q = N Delta Phi / R whatever the history. A 100-turn coil of 50 cm^2 flipped in 0.1 s from face-on to face-on reversed in 0.5 T passes q = 2 Delta Phi N / R weber-turns over R; measure the kick on a ballistic meter and you have B without timing the flip.
Ballistic measurements exploit that charge forgets the rate; current measurements do not.
If the resistance changes during the flip the simple formula fails; integrate the actual i dt instead.
A 100-turn coil of 50 cm2 flipped in 0.5 T passes q = 2 N Delta Phi / R. The ballistic galvanometer reads the charge, not the current.

cards.title: EMF around the loop
items: The EMF is the line integral of the total electric field around the circuit, magnetic and electrostatic parts together. In a uniform-resistance loop the current makes the same fraction of the EMF appear across each segment; in a circuit with a battery the two EMFs add or oppose by their directions around the loop.
Kirchhoff with induction: sum of EMFs equals sum of IR drops; the induced EMF enters as a distributed source around the loop.
An induced EMF distributed around a loop cannot be assigned to one point; only the potential drops of the ohmic parts are local.

cards.title: What the law asserts and assumes
items: \mathcal E=-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf A\ +\ \oint(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l

Faraday law in general has two pieces: a changing field through a stationary circuit, and a moving circuit sweeping flux. The compact flux rule packages both whenever the circuit moves with its material; when the boundary slides through the conductor the package fails and only the charges obey a universal law.
Separating the two mechanisms before substituting is what keeps the sign and the physics straight in mixed problems.
The flux rule is a theorem with hypotheses, not a definition; a sliding contact or a spinning disc needs the charges treatment.

title: Motional EMF: the rod as a battery
subtitle: Conductor moving through uniform B; v, B and the rod mutually perpendicular unless decomposed.
takeaway: A moving rod is a battery of EMF Blv with its positive terminal at the v cross B end; no flux argument is required.

cards.title: From the Lorentz force
items: Free electrons in the moving rod feel q v cross B along the rod and pile up at one end until their electrostatic field balances the magnetic push: qE = qvB gives E = vB inside the rod and a potential difference Blv between the ends. The rod is a battery whose positive terminal is the end toward which v cross B pushes positive charge.
No circuit and no flux were used: the physics is the force on the carriers, valid for a lone rod in space.
The polarity comes from v cross B for positive carriers; never from the current direction elsewhere in the circuit.
A 50 cm rod at 5 m/s in 0.4 T gives 1.0 V; open-circuit, it stands ready with one volt across its ends.

cards.title: The same result from flux
items: With the rod sliding on rails the enclosed area grows at rate lv, so the flux rule gives Blv as well. The two derivations agree because the loop moves with its material; the Lorentz derivation is the physics, the flux rule is the shortcut that packages it.
Two derivations of one number is the check; a disagreement means the flux rule was applied outside its hypotheses.
The flux derivation needs a closed moving loop; the rod alone has EMF between its ends whether or not anything closes the circuit.
d\mathcal E=(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l
A 30 cm rod at 5 m/s in 0.4 T gives 0.6 V.

cards.title: General form and decomposition
items: \mathcal E=\int_{\rm rod}(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l

For a rod at an angle to v or B only the component of v cross B along the rod counts. A rod rotating about one end sweeps elements at different speeds; a rod moving parallel to B generates nothing; a rod moving perpendicular to its own length but at 45 degrees to B takes the sine factor into the integral.
The general integral replaces every special formula; the special formulas are its evaluations.
Blv sin theta uses the angle between v and B; the angle between rod and v cross B is a separate factor. Name both.
Blv at an angle: only the component of v cross B along the rod contributes; decompose before integrating.

cards.title: Where the flux rule needs care
items: \text{follow the charges: } d\mathcal E=(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l

When the circuit boundary slides through the conductor the flux through the circuit is ambiguous: a Faraday disc, a rolling wheel with a rim contact, a contact jumping wires. Compute the force on the charges that actually move; choosing a circuit that rotates with the material restores the flux rule exactly.
The flux rule is exact for loops that carry their material; the Lorentz force is exact always.
A spinning axisymmetric magnet with a still disc gives zero EMF; spin the disc and the magnet may stay or turn with it: only conductor motion counts.
Spinning only the axisymmetric magnet gives zero. The Faraday disc is the flux-rule embarrassment and the Lorentz-force easy victory.

title: Lenz law as energy conservation
subtitle: Any induction problem with a movable part or a changing flux; steady fields.
takeaway: The induced current opposes the change of flux; that sign is the only one consistent with energy conservation.

cards.title: Statement and algorithm
items: Find the change of flux and its sense; the induced current makes a field opposing the change, adding flux when flux is lost and subtracting when it grows; the right-hand rule gives the current; and the mechanical consequence, force or torque, opposes the motion causing the change.
Three steps: change, opposing field, mechanical reaction. The reaction is what makes every generator need a torque to turn.
Lenz opposes the change, not the field: a decreasing inward flux is supported by an induced inward current. Say opposes the change every time.
Closing a switch on a nearby coil: the induced current in the second coil opposes the growth; opening it, the current tries to sustain what is being lost.

cards.title: The energy audit
items: If the induced current attracted the approaching magnet, the magnet would accelerate, the flux would change faster, the current would grow, and energy would appear from nothing. With the correct sign the mechanical work done against the force equals the heat produced: the audit balances and the perpetual machine dies.
Write the ledger before solving: mechanical work in, heat in R, field energy change. It catches every wrong sign.
The audit includes the field energy change when currents are still building; ignoring it is the standard way to lose a minus sign.

cards.title: The magnet in the copper tube
items: A magnet dropped through a conducting tube induces currents in every ring of the wall whose fields oppose the fall; the drag is proportional to speed and the magnet reaches a terminal velocity of tenths of a metre per second, falling like a feather through the tube.
Lenz law you can hold: the demonstration survives every scaling argument because the drag law is linear at these speeds.
The magnet does not stop dead; it approaches a terminal speed. Saying the currents halt the magnet confuses drag with a wall.
Halving the tube radius slows the fall sixteen times: the drag scales as one over a to the fourth for a thin wall.

cards.title: Action and reaction
items: \mathbf F_{\rm on\ rod}=-\mathbf F_{\rm on\ source}

The force on the moving part always opposes the motion relative to the field; the equal and opposite force acts on whatever produces the field. In a generator the crank feels this reaction; in a motor the field feels the reaction of the drive force.
Lenz law is Newton third law written for induction; the pair is always mechanical force and electromagnetic reaction.
The reaction is on the source of B, not on the field itself; track where the momentum goes before writing the balance.
The reaction pair is always mechanical force on the moving part and torque on the source of B. Track the momentum before writing the balance.

title: The rod on rails: coasting and driven
subtitle: Parallel rails distance l apart, uniform B perpendicular, resistance R; frictionless unless stated.
takeaway: The rod family is one first-order equation: exponential decay to rest or exponential approach to a terminal speed.

cards.title: Coasting: the exponential
items: A rod given v0 generates Blv, current Blv/R and retarding force B squared l squared v over R; Newton gives exponential decay with tau = mR over B squared l squared. The rod travels a finite distance v0 tau and dissipates exactly its initial kinetic energy as heat.
One time constant governs the whole family: larger mass or resistance slows the decay, larger B squares it away.
The rod coasts forever in theory but stops within a few tau in practice; the stopping distance is v0 tau, not v0 times some stopping time.

cards.title: Driven: terminal speed
items: A constant force F drives the rod against the same magnetic drag; the speed approaches the terminal value FR over B squared l squared where the applied power Fv is entirely converted to heat. Same tau, same curve shape, inverted: the driven problem is the coasting problem plus a constant.
Both exponentials are the same first-order system seen from two ends; after one tau each has covered 63 per cent of the gap.
The terminal current is F over Bl, not F over R; the mechanical force balance sets the current, and R then sets the speed.

cards.title: The energy ledger
items: At terminal speed every watt of mechanical input is ohmic heat; during the transient the missing part goes into kinetic energy. For the coasting rod the ledger is one-shot: initial kinetic energy equals total Joule heating, provable by integrating B squared l squared v squared over R.
The ledger is the physics; the exponential is just the solution. Check both against each other.
With friction the split between rail heat and resistor heat depends on the whole history; only the total is fixed by energy.
P_{\rm mech}=Fv,\qquad P_{\rm elec}=\mathcal E i=i^2R
At terminal speed the applied power F v equals the Joule heat exactly. The transient stores the missing part as kinetic energy.

cards.title: Time constants compared
items: The rod time constant is mechanical mass over a magnetic drag coefficient; the RL constant is inductance over resistance. They are the same mathematics: both are first-order approaches to a steady state, and both scale linearly with the inertia and the damping inverse.
Recognising one equation in two disguises is the fastest route to the answer in mixed rod-circuit problems.
The rail tau contains no inductance and the RL tau contains no mass; conflating them gives seconds where milliseconds belong.
The rail time constant has no inductance and the RL constant has no mass. Conflating them gives seconds where milliseconds belong.

title: Rotating rods, discs, coils and loops
subtitle: Uniform B perpendicular to the rotation axis; constant omega; thin conductors.
takeaway: Rotation converts a steady field into a sinusoid or a DC voltage: half B omega L squared for a rod, NBA omega for a coil.

cards.title: The rotating rod
items: A rod of length L turning about one end sweeps elements at v = omega r; each contributes B omega r dr and the integral is half B omega L squared, the same as a rod moving at the average speed. A rod pivoted at its centre has zero EMF between its ends but one eighth B omega L squared from centre to either end.
Average-speed thinking reproduces the integral: the midpoint speed times length is the whole answer.
The pivot choice matters: end-pivot gives half B omega L squared, centre-pivot zero end to end. Read the geometry before substituting.
A 0.5 m rod at 100 rad/s in 0.5 T gives 6.25 V; the flux swept per second is the same number in webers.

cards.title: The Faraday disc
items: A spinning disc with brushes at axle and rim is a stack of rotating rods in parallel: a unipolar generator delivering enormous current at a fraction of a volt. Its circuit has no fixed loop; follow the charges or choose a radial line rotating with the disc to make the flux rule work.
The disc is the classic flux-rule embarrassment and the Lorentz-force easy victory; examiners love it precisely for that.
Spinning only the magnet gives zero: an axisymmetric field is unchanged by its own rotation and no charges move through it.
10 cm disc at 300 rad/s in 0.5 T: 0.75 V and, into a milliohm, 750 A with a 1.9 N m braking torque.

cards.title: The rotating coil
items: A coil rotating about its axis in uniform B has Phi = NBA cos omega t and the EMF is the sine, largest when the flux is zero and the sides cut field fastest, zero when the flux peaks. This is the AC generator and the sinusoid every AC section assumes.
The quarter-cycle offset between flux and EMF is the single most-missed fact: maximum flux means zero EMF.
Do not argue EMF is maximum because flux is maximum; differentiate the cosine and watch the sine vanish there.
100 turns, 100 cm^2, 0.2 T at 50 Hz: E0 = 62.8 V and RMS 44 V: the household scale in one line.
A 50 cm disc at 300 rad/s in 0.5 T delivers 0.75 V. Into a milliohm this is 750 A with 1.9 N m braking torque.

cards.title: Loops entering and leaving fields
items: A rectangular loop pulled out of a field region has motional EMF only in the side still inside; wholly inside or outside the two long sides cancel and the flux is constant. A loop sitting still in a changing field has transformer EMF A dB/dt instead: no motion, no motional EMF.
Two EMF species in one picture: motional from motion through B, transformer from changing B through a still loop.
While the loop is wholly inside a uniform field there is no current, even though the field is large; only the boundary crossing matters.
The meter spikes only while an edge crosses the boundary: square pulses separated by quiet gaps.

title: The rod with every attachment
subtitle: Rails joined through R, C, L, a spring or a hanging mass; constant B; one-dimensional motion.
takeaway: Each attachment changes the equation of motion: drag, added mass, damping, or oscillation.

cards.title: Hanging mass
items: A hanging mass M pulls the rod through the pulley; the pair accelerates under Mg minus magnetic drag, reaching terminal speed MgR over B squared l squared with time constant (m+M)R over B squared l squared. At terminal speed the falling weight supplies exactly the resistor heat.
The combined mass sets the approach time; only the hanging weight sets the terminal speed.
The tension is not Mg during acceleration; write Newton for the pair or subtract the two equations, never both inconsistently.
M = 50 g on the 0.5 T circuit gives terminal 4.9 m/s with tau = 1.5 s: half again the coasting time constant.
Tension is not Mg during acceleration.

cards.title: Capacitor instead of resistor
items: With a capacitor there is no steady current; charge q = CBlv grows with the speed and the current is proportional to the acceleration. The magnetic force CB squared l squared dv/dt acts as an added inertia, so the rod accelerates constantly at F over m plus CB squared l squared. No terminal speed exists.
The capacitor rod is a mass problem with extra mass; the current is fixed by the acceleration, not by the speed.
Writing i = Blv/R for a capacitor circuit is the classic error; there is no resistor and the current is set by CBl dv/dt.
B = 2 T, l = 0.5 m, C = 0.1 F, m = 0.1 kg under 1 N: added mass 0.1 kg, a = 5 m/s^2, constant current 0.5 A.

cards.title: Friction and spring
items: Kinetic friction adds a constant opposing force: the coasting rod then stops in finite time, unlike pure magnetic drag. A spring makes a damped oscillator with damping constant B squared l squared over R; replace R by C and the damping disappears into extra mass, leaving slower undamped SHM.
A velocity-proportional drag never stops a body in finite time; a constant one does. That distinction is the whole friction problem.
With a spring the natural frequency is sqrt(k/m) only when the magnetic drag is absent; the damping shifts both amplitude and, lightly, the frequency.

cards.title: Inductor on the rails
items: Rails joined through a pure inductor make the rod oscillate for ever: Blv = L di/dt and m dv/dt = -Bi l combine into SHM with omega = Bl over root(mL). The kinetic energy of the rod exchanges with the inductor field energy: a mass-spring oscillator with the roles renamed.
The rod plays the capacitor in this LC circuit; the analogy table of the inductance sheets reads the answer directly.
No resistance means no decay; adding even a small R turns the oscillation into a ring-down with time constant 2m/b.
The loop equation and Newton combine by differentiation; the first integral is the energy ledger, not another differential equation.

title: Induced electric fields
subtitle: Axisymmetric changing flux, especially a long solenoid of radius R with uniform dB/dt inside.
takeaway: A changing magnetic field makes an electric field that circles the flux; it has no potential and exists where B is zero.

cards.title: The field with no conductor
items: Faraday law without a circuit: a changing B creates an electric field whose circulation around any closed path equals minus the rate of change of flux through it. The field lines close on themselves around the changing region; it is non-conservative and has no potential difference between points.
This is the field the electrostatics rules forbade: closed field lines, non-zero circulation, no potential.
The electrostatic conductor argument fails here; a conductor in a changing flux has circulating induced E and an EMF, not an equipotential body.
\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l=-\int\frac{\partial\mathbf B}{\partial t}\cdot d\mathbf A

cards.title: The solenoid geometry
items: E_{\rm in}=\frac r2\dot B,\qquad E_{\rm out}=\frac{R^2}{2r}\dot B

By symmetry the induced field is azimuthal; a circle of radius r gives E times 2 pi r equal to the enclosed flux rate. Inside, E grows linearly to half R dB/dt at the winding; outside it falls as 1/r where the flux rate is the full solenoid value even though B itself is zero there.
Outside the solenoid there is E with no B: the flux through the loop, not the field on it, is what counts.
The outside field is not zero just because B is zero there; the enclosed flux still changes. Use the full solenoid flux rate for r above R.
R = 5 cm at 100 T/s: E is 1.0 V/m at 2 cm, 2.5 V/m at the winding, 1.25 V/m at 10 cm.
The profile rises linearly inside and falls as 1/r outside. Maximum E sits at the winding itself.

cards.title: A charge accelerated by the induced field
items: A bead on a frictionless ring around the changing flux feels tangential force qE; for r beyond R the impulse per unit charge round the ring is the flux change divided by the circumference, whatever the rate. Free to move on a straight track it accelerates along the track tangent at qE.
The impulse depends on the total flux change, not its rate: the betatron principle in embryo.
The energy gained per revolution is q times the EMF around the ring; the rate of gain depends on dPhi/dt but the per-turn gain does not.
A proton on a 5 cm ring outside a 3 cm solenoid gains 1.3 m/s from a 1e-4 Wb flux rise: rate cancels, impulse does not.

cards.title: Why no potential exists
items: A potential exists only when the circulation vanishes for every loop; here loops enclosing changing flux have circulation minus dPhi/dt. The line integral of E between two points depends on the path by exactly the enclosed flux rate, which is why the word EMF exists and why voltmeters disagree near changing flux.
The voltmeter paradox of the later sheet is this one equation read twice.
Speaking of the potential difference between two points of an inductive loop is undefined until the path is named; use EMF along a stated path.
Two points on the loop have no unique potential difference.

title: The betatron: accelerate with a changing flux
subtitle: Axisymmetric field profile; electrons at fixed orbit radius R; nonrelativistic derivation, relativistic-safe result.
takeaway: The average field inside the orbit must be twice the field on it: the 2:1 condition.

cards.title: Guiding and accelerating, two rates
items: To keep an electron of momentum p on a fixed radius R the orbit field must satisfy p = e B_orb R, so its rate of change must match the momentum gain. The induced field on the orbit is R/2 times the average-field rate; equating the two rates gives the field at the orbit rising at half the average rate.
Two demands on one magnet: bend and accelerate. Equating their rates is the design condition.
Do not confuse the field at the orbit with the average over the disc; the factor of two is exactly that distinction.

cards.title: The 2:1 condition
items: Pole pieces are shaped so the field is stronger inside the orbit than on it. A uniform field fails: momentum then grows only half as fast as the orbit condition demands and the electrons spiral inward. The condition holds at every instant of the ramp, not just on average over the cycle.
A uniform-field betatron is a contradiction in terms; the shaping is the machine.
The classical cyclotron fails for electrons because of relativity; the betatron works because it tracks p = eBR, valid at any speed.
R = 0.5 m with B_orb ramped to 0.5 T in 5 ms: final pc = 75 MeV after 4.8e5 turns of about 157 eV each.

cards.title: The stability window
items: Radial stability needs the available focusing force to fall off more slowly than the 1/r demand: n below 1. Vertical stability needs the field lines to bow outward: n above 0. Weak focusing lives in the window between; the same n keeps the 2:1 profile satisfied across the orbit.
One exponent decides whether the beam stays put; machine design is this inequality made of steel.
A perfectly uniform field (n = 0) fails vertical stability too: the beam is free to drift out of the mid-plane.
Displace an electron outward at fixed p: centripetal demand falls as 1/r, supply as r^-n; restoring needs n below 1.
Displace the orbit outward at fixed p: the demand falls as 1/r while the supply falls as r to the minus n.

cards.title: Energy accounting
items: Each turn the electron gains e times the flux rate, about 157 eV in the worked machine; the total after half a million turns is the 75 MeV set by e B_orb R c. The argument used p throughout, which is why relativity costs nothing here.
Accounting by turns checks the ramp: gain per turn times turns must equal the final p c.
The betatron does not need a fixed frequency; the orbit period changes as the electron speeds up and nothing resonates.
The argument used p throughout, which is why the betatron works for electrons where the cyclotron fails. Gains of 157 eV per turn over 4.8e5 turns give 75 MeV.

title: Eddy currents: braking, heating and laminating
subtitle: Conductors in non-uniform or changing fields; ohmic metal of conductivity sigma and density rho_m.
takeaway: Eddy currents oppose the change that makes them; their drag is proportional to speed and their heat scales with the square of thickness.

cards.title: Magnetic braking
items: A plate moving through a field edge drives current density sigma v B through the metal; dissipated power fixes a retarding force proportional to speed. The velocity decays exponentially with a time constant depending on material and field, not on the plate size: tau about rho_m over k sigma B squared.
The brake is a velocity-proportional drag: it never stops a body in finite time by itself, only exponentially.
Constant friction stops in finite time; eddy drag does not. Keep the two regimes distinct in every stopping problem.
Copper in 0.5 T with k = 0.1 gives tau about 6 ms; aluminium, with half the rho/sigma, stops twice as fast.

cards.title: The slotted pendulum
items: A solid copper bob swinging between magnet poles stops within one swing; slot the bob so the eddy paths are cut, k collapses, and it swings freely. The demonstration is the lamination principle in one motion: interrupt the current loops and the loss dies.
Every eddy-current remedy is the same move: break the loop paths with slots, laminations or gaps.
The slot must cut across the current direction; a slot parallel to the currents changes nothing.
A 50 g bob at 0.5 T is far past critical damping: it returns to rest without overshooting.
The slotted bob keeps its mass and loses its eddy paths. At 0.02 T the bob keeps about 8 visible swings; at 0.5 T it stops in one.

cards.title: Induction heating and skin depth
items: An alternating field drives eddy currents whose power grows with frequency squared until the skin effect confines them to a depth delta. At 25 kHz iron has delta about 0.1 mm: the current concentrates in a thin high-resistance skin and the pan heats. Aluminium at the same frequency has delta about 0.5 mm and mostly reflects the field.
Induction hobs need ferromagnetic pans not for coupling but for resistance: the skin must be thin.
The power law holds below the skin-effect regime only; quoting f squared at megahertz without delta is a trap.
The power law holds below the skin-effect regime only. Iron at 25 kHz has 0.1 mm skin: thin and resistive, which is why the pan heats.

cards.title: Laminations: the d squared law
items: A core slab of thickness d carrying B0 cos omega t parallel to its faces develops E = x dB/dt at depth x; averaging sigma E squared gives power per volume proportional to d squared. Cutting the core into sheets ten times thinner reduces eddy loss a hundredfold: 0.35 mm silicon steel at 1.2 T and 50 Hz loses 0.19 W/kg where the solid core would glow.
The square law is why transformer and motor cores are laminated, painted and packed.
Hysteresis loss is the other half of core heating and scales with frequency, not with d squared; the two losses have different remedies.
Same core solid at 2 cm thick: 4.7 MW/m^3 against 1.45 kW/m^3 laminated — a factor of 3300.

title: Generators, motors and back-EMF
subtitle: Coils in uniform B driven at constant omega; armature resistance R; steady load.
takeaway: A generator under load is hard to turn because its own current reacts on the crank; a motor under load slows because back-EMF falls.

cards.title: The AC generator
items: A rotating coil delivers a sinusoid of peak NBA omega; the EMF is largest when the sides cut field fastest, which is when the flux through the coil is zero. Large power stations turn a magnet inside fixed coils at 50 or 60 Hz; the frequency is set by the turbine speed and the pole count.
Faraday plus rotation is the whole generator; the phase offset between flux and EMF is the exam favourite.
Maximum EMF at zero flux, not maximum flux; this inversion is checked by differentiating the flux.
Peak EMF occurs at zero flux: the sides cut field fastest when the coil is edge-on. Differentiate the cosine to see the sine vanish at maximum flux.

cards.title: Commutation and motors
items: A DC motor uses a commutator to flip the coil connections twice per turn; a DC generator the same device in reverse. In a running motor the back-EMF opposes the supply: V minus E equals IR, so the current is set by how fast the motor turns, not by R alone.
Back-EMF is Faraday fighting the supply; the armature current is the difference divided by R.
A stalled motor has zero back-EMF and draws V/R: 24 A for a 12 V motor at 0.5 ohm, enough to burn it in seconds.
12 V motor with 0.5 ohm: 24 A at start, 4 A running at back-EMF 10 V. The stall current is the design limit.
A stalled motor draws V / R: 24 A for a 12 V motor at 0.5 ohm.

cards.title: Why a generator gets harder to turn
items: \tau_{\rm mech}=\frac{\mathcal E i}{\omega},\qquad P_{\rm mech}=\mathcal E i=i^2(R+R_{\rm int})

The armature current in the field feels a torque opposing the rotation; the crank supplies exactly the electrical power delivered plus the coil heat. Open the circuit and the crank turns freely; short it and it is hardest of all. A brighter bulb means a smaller load resistance, more current and more torque.
The hand on the crank pays for every watt: mechanical input equals electrical output plus losses, identically.
The opposition torque scales with the current; confusing it with friction loses the whole load dependence.
A generator feeding a battery pushes against its voltage: the shaft supplies exactly E times I.

cards.title: Regenerative braking and pickups
items: Run the traction motor as a generator and the car recharges its battery while the current torque slows it: Lenz law as fuel saving. A guitar pickup is a magnet and coil around a steel string whose vibration changes the flux at the string frequency; a dynamic microphone is the same coil run backwards.
Devices are chapters in hardware: motor, generator and pickup are one Lorentz-force family.
A pickup needs a ferromagnetic string to concentrate the flux; nylon strings give almost no signal.
The loudspeaker is the motor principle on a coil in a radial field; reverse the current and it becomes the microphone.

title: The voltmeter paradox and everyday induction
subtitle: Loops containing changing flux; real voltmeter leads forming their own loops.
takeaway: With changing flux inside a circuit, two voltmeters on the same two points can legitimately read different numbers.

cards.title: Two voltmeters, two readings
items: A loop of two resistors around a changing flux carries one current; a voltmeter whose leads bow left encloses part of the flux and reads the IR drop minus that EMF; leads bowing right enclose the rest and read the opposite residual. Both readings are correct line integrals of E along their own paths.
The voltmeter measures the line integral along its leads; with induction the answer depends on the path.
There is no error in the meters and no paradox in the physics: the question the meters answer is path-dependent by construction.

cards.title: EMF is not a potential difference
items: Between two points of an inductive circuit the integral of E depends on which way the path goes around, by exactly the enclosed flux rate. Potential difference exists only where the circulation vanishes; with changing flux it does not, and the word EMF names what does exist.
The word potential should not be used for an induced EMF; the correct object is an EMF along a named path.
Keep voltmeter leads twisted and away from changing flux, or accept that you are measuring the flux.

cards.title: Induction around us
items: Metal detectors read eddy-current loading of a search coil; induction hobs heat the pan as a shorted secondary; wireless charging is a transformer with an air gap; maglev lifts via induced track currents; regenerative braking runs the motor backwards. One law, a dozen devices.
Every device is one of the four Faraday experiments in production form.
Device vocabulary hides the physics; translate each demo into flux change before computing.
The coin detector signal falls as one over distance to the sixth: dipole coupling, not the inverse square law.
Large search coils see deep and coarse, small coils fine and shallow: the detectorist trades depth for resolution.

cards.title: The energy path
items: No charge crosses a transformer; the energy travels in the fields around the core. The wires guide the Poynting flux from source to load; in a DC circuit too the energy flows through the air around the wire and enters the resistor through its surface.
Field energy transport is the honest picture; the wire is a guide, not a conveyor belt.
Asking where the energy is in a circuit: in the fields, with the sources and sinks at the ends.
The same E cross H flux carries power along a coaxial cable at the speed of the wave front.
The Poynting vector near a coax points along the gap and integrates to exactly EI at every cross-section.

title: Flux linkage and self-inductance
subtitle: Coils of N turns in vacuum or linear media; steady geometry; current I.
takeaway: A coil resists changes in its own current; its measure is the flux linkage per ampere: L = N Phi / I.

cards.title: The definition
items: Close a switch and the current does not jump: the growing flux induces an EMF opposing the growth. Open it and the collapsing flux drives the current on, the spark. The henry is one weber per ampere: a 1 H coil makes 1 V when its current changes at 1 A/s.
Inductance is electrical inertia; the definition mirrors the capacitor but resists current change instead of voltage.
L = N Phi / I with Phi the flux through ONE turn: N enters twice, hence L grows as N squared.
The 10 mH coil on 20 V through 10 ohm settles in about a millisecond; resistance alone sets the final 2 A.

cards.title: Geometry alone
items: Because B is proportional to I for steady currents in vacuum, L is pure geometry: turns, size, shape. A 200-turn coil of the same shape has four times the inductance of a 100-turn coil. The exception is a ferromagnetic core whose mu depends on B; iron-cored L falls as the core saturates.
Scaling by N squared answers half the exam questions without any integration.
Saturating iron makes L current-dependent; quote the small-signal value and state the assumption.
Doubling the turns doubles the field and doubles the linkage: the square law is two factors of N.
Iron-cored L falls as the core saturates: quote the small-signal value and state the assumption. A 200-turn coil has four times the inductance of a 100-turn coil.

cards.title: Where the energy lives
items: The energy is in the field, not the wire: half L I squared equals the B squared over 2 mu0 integrated over all space. A gapped core stores most of its energy in the gap even though the winding is on the iron: field energy follows B squared times volume.
Saying the energy is in the coil is the bookkeeping error behind most wrong gap estimates.
A small inductance can store large energy at large current; energy scales as I squared, inductance linearly.
A 10 H magnet at 500 A stores 1.25 MJ: the kinetic energy of a 1.5-tonne car at 150 km/h.
Doubling the gap roughly doubles the stored energy at the same flux before saturation: the gap buys headroom.

cards.title: Real inductors
items: Every real coil has winding resistance in series and turn-to-turn capacitance in parallel; the two resonate at a self-resonant frequency above which the inductor behaves as a capacitor. Cores add saturation and hysteresis; high-frequency coils are air-cored or ferrite, small and wound to minimise capacitance.
The ideal formulas are exact for idealised geometry and a good first estimate; the parasitics decide the usable band.
Above self-resonance the impedance rises again: the component has stopped being an inductor.

title: Computing L: four standard geometries
subtitle: Long solenoid, toroid, coaxial cable, two-wire line; vacuum or uniform core.
takeaway: Inductance is flux linkage per ampere computed from the geometry: mu0 n squared A l for a solenoid.

cards.title: The long solenoid
items: B = mu0 n I links each of N turns through area A: L = mu0 n squared A l. The per-litre view L/V = mu0 n squared is the useful thinking: a given winding density gives a given inductance per unit volume. With a mu_r core multiply, below saturation.
Compute the flux through one turn, multiply by N, divide by I; the same recipe works for every geometry.
Using n instead of N in the numerator is the common slip; check dimensions: mu0 n squared A l has henrys.
1000 turns on 20 cm of 2 cm radius: L = 7.9 mH in air.
The per-litre view L / V = mu0 n squared gives inductance per winding volume.

cards.title: Toroid and coaxial cable
items: The toroid is the solenoid bent shut: L = mu0 N squared A / 2 pi r, with no external field. The coax cable has flux per length mu0 I ln(b/a) / 2 pi in its gap annulus: L prime = mu0 ln(b/a) / 2 pi, about 0.32 microhenry per metre for b/a = 5.
Both are one flux integral; the toroid hides its ends and the coax hides its return path.
The cable inductance omits the flux inside the conductors, a small low-frequency correction of mu0 / 8 pi per conductor.
The toroid confines every field line inside the winding: zero in the hole and outside. The coax puts all its flux in the gap annulus.

cards.title: Two-wire line and single loop
items: A two-wire line of spacing d and wire radius a has mu0 ln(d/a) / pi per length; a single loop of radius R and wire radius a has L about mu0 R times the logarithm of 8R/a minus 2: 0.59 microhenry for R = 10 cm and a = 1 mm. Every loop is about a microhenry per metre of wire.
The logarithm is the signature of flux inside a geometry with one small dimension.
The single-loop formula diverges logarithmically as the wire thins: real answers always quote the wire radius.
Doubling the coax outer radius adds only 0.14 microhenry per metre: cables of very different sizes have similar impedances.
A single loop diverges logarithmically as the wire thins; real answers always quote the wire radius.

cards.title: L prime C prime and the speed
items: With the capacitors note C prime = 2 pi eps0 / ln(b/a) for the same cable: the product L prime C prime is mu0 eps0, so signals travel at the speed of light in the dielectric, independent of geometry. The ratio gives the characteristic impedance 60 ln(b/a) ohms divided by root kappa.
The cable pair L prime, C prime carries the whole transmission-line story: speed from the product, impedance from the ratio.
Only the impedance depends on b/a; the speed depends on the dielectric alone.
Going from b over a = 2 to b over a = 4 adds just 60 ln 2 = 42 ohm: the geometry factor is logarithmic.

title: Mutual inductance and coupling
subtitle: Two coils; linear media; current in one linking flux through the other.
takeaway: Mutual inductance is reciprocity: M12 = M21, so compute it the easy way round.

cards.title: Definition and reciprocity
items: A current in coil 1 links flux through coil 2; linkage per ampere is M. Reciprocity M12 = M21 is a theorem of the double integral of dl1 dot dl2 over r, symmetric in the two loops. Compute the easy direction: current in the long solenoid, flux through the small coil, never the reverse.
Reciprocity converts hard problems into easy ones; the small coil inside a long solenoid is the archetype.
The EMF in the secondary opposes the CHANGE of primary current; a steady primary current gives no secondary EMF.
M is bounded by root(L1 L2): perfect coupling on a shared core, less in air.
Reciprocity lets you compute M the easy way round: current in the long solenoid, flux through the small coil.

cards.title: Coaxial solenoids
items: A second winding over a length of a long solenoid links B1 = mu0 n1 I1 through N2 turns of area A1: M = mu0 n1 N2 A1. With both windings sharing the same flux path M reaches root(L1 L2); the coupling coefficient k measures the fraction of flux shared.
One formula and one bound; every transformer question is somewhere between them.
A transformer needs k near 1 on a shared iron core; air-coupled side-by-side coils run k = 0.1 to 0.5.
Both windings sharing one flux path give M = root(L1 L2). Air-coupled side-by-side coils run k = 0.1 to 0.5; a shared iron core approaches 1.

cards.title: When M vanishes
items: Two coils whose axes are perpendicular with coincident centres share no flux however close: M = 0. Radio circuits use this to decouple coils. A rectangle beside a long wire has M = mu0 a ln((d+b)/d) / 2 pi, computed from the flux integral of the flux sheet.
The zero-coupling geometry is the standard true/false question; the answer follows from the flux, not the distance.
M depends on orientation, not proximity; moving coils closer does not help if the flux threading is zero.
Near a straight wire the mutual inductance is the flux per ampere: one integral answers both readings.
Orthogonal pick-up coils on the same axis have M = 0 to first order: this is how receivers reject cross-talk.

cards.title: Energy of coupled coils
items: Two coils carrying I1 and I2 store their self energies plus a mutual term with the sign of the flux linkage. Holding currents constant the force on a movable coil is plus one half I squared dM/dx; holding flux constant the same force appears with the source disconnected.
The sign of the mutual term is the sign of the shared flux: aiding currents add energy, opposing subtract.
The force law needs the CURRENTS fixed by sources for the plus sign; isolated coils conserve flux and the bookkeeping flips.
The sign of the mutual term follows the shared flux. Aiding currents add energy, opposing subtract; measuring both series forms yields M without geometry.

title: The RL circuit and the inductive kick
subtitle: Series R and L with battery V; switch at t = 0; no mutual coupling.
takeaway: Current cannot jump in an inductor; the exponential joins the states at rate tau = L/R.

cards.title: Rise: the exponential
items: Kirchhoff gives V = iR + L di/dt; the current rises from zero to V/R with time constant L/R. The inductor takes the full voltage at first and none at last; the resistor does the opposite. Check by substitution: L di/dt and iR sum to V at every instant.
Initial and final states first, then the exponential joins them: the inductor is an open circuit at t = 0 and a wire at infinity.
The time constant uses the resistance the current ACTUALLY flows through after the switch; a different R before and after is the standard trap.
10 mH and 5 ohm on 10 V: tau = 2 ms, final 2 A, half-current after 1.4 ms.

cards.title: Decay
items: Short the battery out and the inductor drives the decaying current; its voltage reverses and the stored half L I squared appears as heat in R. The integral of i squared R equals the initial field energy exactly: the audit closes.
The inductor becomes the source during decay; the polarity of its voltage flips.
Never leave the current path open when switching off a large inductance; give it a path or pay the voltage.
A freewheel diode gives the decaying current a safe path: the same L over R physics, with no arc at the switch.

cards.title: The inductive kick
items: Interrupt 2 A in 10 mH within a microsecond and 20 kV appears across the opening contacts: the air breaks down, an arc carries the current until the energy is spent, and the contacts erode. The flyback diode gives the current a harmless path; the snubber capacitor turns the kick into an LC ring.
The energy always goes somewhere: arc, diode loop, snubber, or spark. Name the victim in every switching problem.
The kick is a voltage spike from a small energy; it is the short time, not the joules, that breaks down the gap.
An ignition coil exploits the same spike with a 1:100 turns ratio: 20 to 30 kV at the spark plug.

cards.title: Slow charging of big magnets
items: Charging time scales as L times I over V: doubling the target current doubles the wait, whatever the resistance. Discharging faster than the supply allows needs somewhere to put megajoules; a quench dump resistor is that somewhere. The current rate is set by V/L, not by R.
Large inductances make slow machines; the ramp rate is a design parameter, not an afterthought.
With superconducting windings R is zero and the steady state is whatever the current reached; tau = L/R is meaningless there.
The stored half L I squared at 500 A in 10 H is 1.25 MJ; the dump resistor must swallow it as heat.
A superconducting magnet of 10 H charged from 10 V rises at 1 A/s: 500 A takes eight minutes.

title: Energy in the magnetic field
subtitle: Linear media; long solenoid or toroid geometry; uniform field inside.
takeaway: Half L I squared is B squared over 2 mu0 per unit volume of field: magnetic storage beats electric by five decades.

cards.title: From circuit to field
items: While the current rises the source works against the back-EMF at rate L i di/dt; integrating gives half L I squared. Applied to the solenoid L = mu0 n squared A l and B = mu0 n I this becomes B squared over 2 mu0 times the interior volume: the energy lives in the field.
Two expressions for one energy: use the circuit form for bookkeeping and the field form for where it sits.
The field form integrates over ALL space; for a long solenoid the interior dominates and the formula is nearly exact.
The circuit form handles bookkeeping; the field form says where the energy sits.

cards.title: Electric versus magnetic storage
items: Air breaks down at 3 MV/m giving 40 J per cubic metre electric; 1 T is routine and gives 0.4 MJ per cubic metre magnetic. Capacitor or inductor, the same bookkeeping: half C V squared against half L I squared, with the mirror-image rule that capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot jump.
Field storage means magnetic fields; electric fields are limited by breakdown long before.
Comparing storage at equal breakdown margins is the fair test; at equal volume magnetic wins overwhelmingly.
The MRI magnet of 1.5 T over a cubic metre holds about 0.9 MJ per cubic metre: a car crash worth of energy in a bore.

cards.title: What cannot jump
items: A capacitor holds its voltage through a switching instant; an inductor holds its current. This one rule fixes every initial condition: at t = 0 plus, i_L equals i_L before and V_C equals V_C before. The currents and voltages of the OTHER element can jump freely.
Continuity bookkeeping replaces solving at the instant; write the state table before the differential equations.
Energy is NOT continuous at a switch; sparks and arcs are the visible proof.
Closing a switch on a charged capacitor wastes exactly half the stored energy in the leads every time.

cards.title: The pressure reading
items: Magnetic pressure equals energy density: 4 atmospheres at 1 T, 400 at 10 T. The winding of a solenoid carries this pressure as tension; the gapped core stores most of its energy in the gap where the field volume is.
Pressure and energy density sharing one expression is why magnet design is pressure-vessel design.
The pressure acts on the confining currents, not on free charges; it is the field pushing on its own container.
1 T over 10 cm squared end area pulls the halves together with 400 N: pressure times area.
The pressure acts on the confining currents, not on free charges. A 1 T solenoid of 10 cm2 bore pulls its halves together with 400 N.

title: The mechanical-electrical analogy and combinations
subtitle: Linear elements; single loop or pair of coupled coils; ohmic R.
takeaway: Every circuit equation has a mechanical twin: mass is inductance, spring is capacitance, dashpot is resistance.

cards.title: The table
items: Displacement is charge, velocity is current, force is EMF. Mass cannot change velocity abruptly exactly as inductance cannot change current; the spring force is the capacitor voltage; the dashpot is the resistor. Read tau = m/b as L/R and omega0 = root(k/m) as 1/root(LC).
The analogy reads unfamiliar circuits off known mechanics in one line: the capacitor rod is an added mass, the RL circuit a falling body.
The analogy fails for mutual coupling: no mechanical element does what M does, and it says nothing about where the energy lives.

cards.title: Series and parallel
items: Without coupling series adds and parallel combines by reciprocals, like resistors but because flux linkages add. With shared flux the series pair gains or loses 2M depending on whether the windings aid; two identical coils in opposition on one core give zero inductance.
The non-inductive winding is two coils subtracting their flux: precision resistors are wound that way.
The sign of M is set by the winding sense relative to the shared axis; drawing both currents clockwise is not enough.
Perfect coupling gives (root L1 plus or minus root L2) squared: check both limits against zero and infinite M.
Two 1 mH coils on one core give 4 mH aiding and nearly zero opposed: the non-inductive winding again.

cards.title: Energy of coupled coils
items: The cross term is the work of establishing the mutual flux against the other coil. Its derivative at fixed current gives the force between the coils; at fixed flux the source is absent and the sign flips. Both bookkeepings give the same physical force.
One force law, two ledgers: quote the constraint before the derivative.
Series aiding and opposing give the two observed inductances; measuring both yields M without any geometry.
The cross term is the work of establishing mutual flux. At fixed current the force is one half I squared dM/dx; at fixed flux the source is absent and the ledger flips.

cards.title: The inductor pair switched
items: Switch a current-carrying L1 across an uncharged L2 with negligible resistance: flux linkage is conserved, giving a common current, while a fraction of the energy is lost to the switching arc however small the resistance. The inductive twin of the two-capacitor loss.
Flux conservation sets the final state; the loss is the price of the switch, and only the mechanism depends on R.
Energy is not conserved in the joining; linkage is. State both before substituting.
10 mH at 3 A into 20 mH: final 1 A, energy falls 45 to 15 mJ, losing 30 mJ.
Reopening the switch after the join forces the same flux through an arc: the spark energy is the 30 mJ deficit.

title: LC oscillations and flux conservation
subtitle: Ideal LC with no resistance, then small R; superconducting loops; switching transients.
takeaway: The LC circuit is simple harmonic motion: charge is displacement, inductance is mass, capacitance is the spring.

cards.title: The oscillator
items: With no resistance the loop rule is L di/dt plus q/C = 0: SHM at omega0 = 1/root(LC). The current peaks a quarter-cycle after the charge; the energy sloshes between q squared / 2C and half L i squared, constant in sum, equal twice per cycle.
The quarter-cycle phase between charge and current is the AC section arriving early.
The frequency uses the LOOP inductance and capacitance; stray wiring adds both and shifts the answer.
10 mH and 100 nF ring at 5.0 kHz with I0 = 0.32 A from 10 microcoulomb at 100 V.

cards.title: Ring-down with resistance
items: Small R makes a damped oscillator: the amplitude decays with time constant 2L/R while the energy decays with L/R; the ringing lasts about Q cycles. Below critical resistance the circuit still oscillates; above, it creeps.
The quality factor counts the visible oscillations; a coil of Q = 157 rings a few hundred cycles.
There is no tau = L/R exponential approach in LC circuits; two storage elements oscillate instead.
Below critical resistance the circuit still oscillates; above, it creeps. A coil of 10 mH with 2 ohm at 5 kHz has Q = 157 and rings hundreds of cycles.

cards.title: Flux conservation
items: A zero-resistance loop keeps its flux linkage: any attempt to change it induces exactly the current that cancels the change. A switched inductor pair conserves L1 I0 across both; a squashed superconducting ring raises its current as L falls; a magnet dropped at a ring floats.
Flux linkage is the momentum of the superconducting loop; use it for the final state and an energy audit for the loss.
Flux conservation holds for times short compared with L/R in ordinary circuits; afterwards Faraday with R applies.
Squash a 1 microhenry ring at 100 A to half its inductance: the current doubles to 200 A and the energy rises 5 to 10 mJ.

cards.title: The mechanical twins
items: A mass on a spring is an LC circuit in disguise; the four snapshots of the oscillation map exactly: fully charged is maximum displacement, maximum current is maximum velocity. Damping maps to resistance and the driven case maps to forced oscillation with resonance.
Reading the mechanical picture solves circuit questions faster than the algebra when the geometry is unfamiliar.
The analogy maps energy locations wrongly: the mass KE is the inductor field, not the wire energy.
The equal-energy instant is 45 degrees of phase, twice per cycle: same as the mass-spring equipartition crossing.

title: Why AC, and what RMS means
subtitle: Sinusoidal sources; periodic waveforms; resistive heating as the definition of effective current.
takeaway: The mains number is the RMS: 230 V is 325 V peak in disguise, and the effective current heats like DC.

cards.title: Where AC comes from
items: Every large generator is a rotating coil or magnet at fixed speed: 50 Hz in India and Europe, 60 Hz in the Americas. AC won because only a changing flux drives a transformer and only a transformer can step voltage up for transmission and down for use. Vocabulary: peak V0, peak-to-peak 2V0, period, frequency, phase.
The transformer is why AC exists; the sinusoid is what rotation gives for free.
The rated 230 V is neither peak nor average; appliances must survive the 325 V peak.
Only a changing flux drives a transformer; only a transformer makes high-voltage transmission practical. The sinusoid comes free from rotation.

cards.title: RMS from heating
items: The effective current is the steady current that heats a resistor at the same average rate; squaring removes the sign, averaging uses sin squared = 1/2, and the root gives I0 over root 2. The 230 V mains figure is an RMS value: its 325 V peak is what the insulation must survive.
RMS is defined by heating, not by calculus fashion; every waveform has its own factor.
Mixing one peak and one RMS value in one formula is wrong by root 2; mixing two is wrong by 2.
230 V RMS is 325 V peak; a capacitor rated 250 V across the mains fails.
RMS values multiply like DC: P = I rms squared R.

cards.title: Average versus RMS
items: The full-cycle average of a sinusoid is zero, which is why DC meters read nothing on AC. The half-cycle average is 2/pi of the peak: the reading of a DC meter fed through a full-wave rectifier. It is NOT the RMS: 0.637 against 0.707, and a meter calibrated for sinusoids misreads other waveforms.
Two different means of one sine: the arithmetic mean of the rectified wave and the root-mean-square of the raw wave.
A moving-coil meter on a rectifier reads 0.90 of true RMS for sine input; the calibration is waveform-specific.

cards.title: Other waveforms
items: From the definition: a square wave of amplitude I0 has RMS I0 since i squared is constant; a triangular wave gives I0 over root 3; a half-wave rectified sinusoid gives I0/2 with average I0 over pi; a full-wave rectified sinusoid keeps the sine RMS I0 over root 2. Each waveform carries its own pair of factors.
Compute from the definition once and the factors become recognisable shortcuts.
Never assume 0.707 for non-sinusoidal AC; the defining integral is the only safe route.
Half-wave rectified: RMS I0/2, average I0/pi; full-wave: RMS I0/root 2, average 2I0/pi.

title: R, L and C on AC: amplitude and phase
subtitle: Each element alone across v = V0 sin omega t; linear; constant L and C.
takeaway: Each element sets its own amplitude and phase: R in phase, L lagging 90 degrees, C leading 90 degrees.

cards.title: The resistor
items: Ohm point by point: the current is in phase with the voltage and its amplitude is V0/R. No phase puzzle and no energy storage; the resistor dissipates at the instantaneous rate i squared R whose average is I rms squared R.
The resistor is the reference phasor: everything else is measured against its phase.
Instantaneous Ohm law still holds; using peak values in it is fine as long as both sides are peaks.
Ohm point by point with peaks is fine as long as both sides are peaks. The resistor is the reference phasor; everything else is measured against its phase.

cards.title: The inductor
items: From v = L di/dt the current is the integral of a sine, a negative cosine: amplitude V0 / omega L and a phase lag of 90 degrees. Physically the inductor is inertia: push and the velocity builds after. X_L = omega L grows with frequency: an inductor blocks high frequencies and passes DC.
The integral explains the lag; the inertia picture remembers it.
X_L is not a resistance: the element stores and returns energy, dissipating nothing.
50 mH at 50 Hz gives X_L = 15.7 ohm; at 5 kHz it is 1571 ohm: two decades of frequency swap the roles.

cards.title: The capacitor
items: From q = Cv the current is the derivative: amplitude omega C V0 and a phase lead of 90 degrees. The current must flow first to build the charge that makes the voltage. X_C = 1/omega C falls with frequency: a capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies.
Derivative gives the lead; the spring picture: force is largest at maximum displacement, when the flow is zero.
The mnemonic CIVIL holds: in C, I before V; in L, V before I.
10 microfarad at 50 Hz gives X_C = 318 ohm; at 5 kHz only 3.2 ohm: L small and C large at mains frequency.

cards.title: Reactance is not resistance
items: A pure L or C limits current amplitude but dissipates no average power: over a cycle the element takes energy from the source for a quarter period and returns it the next. Only R dissipates. The phase between v and i is the whole story of the next sheets.
Reactance sets amplitude; the phase decides power. Keep the two questions separate.
Do not add X_L and R as scalars; the next sheets combine them as perpendicular phasors.
At resonance the reactances cancel and the source sees pure resistance: the preview of the LCR sheet.
A capacitor passes current while the voltage is already falling: that is why the current leads, never lags.

title: Phasors: sinusoids as rotating vectors
subtitle: Single frequency omega; linear circuits; amplitudes and phases constant in time.
takeaway: Two sinusoids of the same frequency add as vectors: that is why phasor diagrams work.

cards.title: The construction
items: A sinusoid is the vertical projection of a vector of length A rotating anticlockwise at omega from initial angle alpha. Projection is linear, so the sum of two sinusoids of one frequency is the vector sum of their phasors; freezing the common rotation leaves a static diagram.
Linearity of projection is the legitimacy; at two frequencies the method fails and solutions superpose instead.
Draw phasors anticlockwise; the projection is onto the vertical axis in the convention used here.
Two equal phasors 120 degrees apart add to one of the same length: the three-phase sum is zero.

cards.title: Series circuits: current is common
items: In a series circuit the current is shared, so draw its phasor along the reference axis. Then V_R lies along I, V_L is rotated 90 degrees ahead, V_C 90 degrees behind. Their vector sum is the source phasor; its length is the voltage amplitude and its angle is the phase by which voltage leads current.
One current, three voltage phasors: the whole series analysis is geometry.
Voltages across the elements are at different phases; the source is their vector sum, never their arithmetic sum.
The source phasor is the vector sum of element voltages.

cards.title: The three triangles
items: Series RC: the source voltage lags the current by arctan(X_C/R); series RL leads by arctan(X_L/R); series LC has V_L and V_C antiparallel and the source is their difference, vanishing when X_L = X_C: resonance before it is named. Each is a right-angled triangle of phasors.
Three standard triangles; every series question is one of them or the full LCR triangle next.
The sign of phi follows which reactance dominates; the arctan argument is always the net reactance over R.
In series RC the current leads the source; in RL it lags. The capacitor leads, the inductor lags: CIVIL again.

cards.title: Parallel circuits: voltage is common
items: In a parallel circuit the voltage is shared: draw V as reference and the branch currents as phasors. I_R lies along V, I_C leads by 90 degrees, I_L lags by 90 degrees; the line current is their vector sum. Branch currents do not add as numbers.
The mirror construction of the series case: swap the roles of current and voltage.
Ammeters in the branches read magnitudes only; the line current is the phasor sum and can be smaller than either branch.
With any two of the three voltages known, the phasor triangle closes the third: draw before you compute.

title: Series LCR: impedance and phase
subtitle: R, L, C in series on v = V0 sin omega t; linear; steady state at one frequency.
takeaway: Impedance Z is the phasor sum of R and net reactance; voltages across the elements do not add as numbers.

cards.title: The impedance triangle
items: The common current carries V_R along it and the net reactive voltage perpendicular; the source amplitude is their vector sum, defining impedance Z. The phase phi by which voltage leads current is positive when the circuit is inductive, negative when capacitive. The triangle has R on the base, net reactance vertical, Z as hypotenuse.
One triangle gives amplitude and phase at once; drawing it prevents the scalar-addition error.
Z is not the sum of R, X_L and X_C; the reactances subtract first and enter as a leg.
One triangle gives amplitude and phase at once. The phase is positive when inductive, negative when capacitive; Z is never the arithmetic sum.

cards.title: Voltages do not add
items: A voltmeter across L may read more than the source; the readings of the three elements at 50 Hz in the worked circuit are 15, 12 and 242 V against a 230 V source. The phasor sum is 230 V exactly; the arithmetic sum 269 V is meaningless. Each of V_L and V_C can exceed the source: the magnification of the resonance sheet.
Read the meters as phasor magnitudes; only resistive runs add as numbers.
The classic trap: adding inductive and capacitive voltages that are 180 degrees apart; read their difference.
20 ohm, 50 mH, 10 microfarad at 50 Hz: Z = 303 ohm, I = 0.76 A, phi = -86 degrees: almost a pure capacitor.

cards.title: The worked circuit
items: At 50 Hz the net reactance is -302 ohm: the circuit is capacitive and the current leads by 86 degrees. At 225 Hz the reactances cancel and the same circuit resonates with Z = R = 20 ohm and eleven times the current. One circuit, two characters, set by frequency.
Frequency decides which element dominates; computing both extremes exposes the physics.
The resonance frequency uses L and C only; R moves the peak width, not its location.
One circuit, two characters: 225 Hz resonance with Z = 20 ohm against 50 Hz with Z = 303 ohm. Frequency decides which element dominates.

cards.title: Reading the phase
items: The sign of phi tells the character: below resonance X_C dominates and current leads; above, X_L dominates and current lags; at resonance phi = 0 and the source sees a pure resistance. The phase is measurable as the time shift between voltage and current zero-crossings.
Three regimes, one sign test; exam questions often ask only which way the phase points.
At exact resonance the voltages across L and C are equal and opposite, not zero each.
Half-cycle shift of 86 degrees is about 2.4 ms at 50 Hz: measurable on an oscilloscope.
Half of an 86 degree shift is about 2.4 ms at 50 Hz: measurable on a scope. At exact resonance the L and C voltages are equal and opposite.

title: Resonance, Q and bandwidth
subtitle: Series LCR driven at variable frequency; linear; steady state.
takeaway: A circuit driven at its natural frequency responds most; Q measures both the magnification and the sharpness.

cards.title: The resonance condition
items: When X_L equals X_C the impedance is least, the current is greatest and the phase vanishes: the source sees a pure resistance. This is the LC oscillator natural frequency: a circuit driven at the frequency it would ring at by itself responds most. Below omega0 the circuit is capacitive, above it inductive.
Resonance is the driven oscillator finding its own frequency; the peak of I(omega) is the fingerprint.
Parallel LC resonates at the same frequency with maximum impedance and minimum line current: the opposite response.

cards.title: Voltage magnification
items: At resonance V_L equals V_C equals I0 X_L: with Q = 50 a 10 V source puts 500 V across the capacitor. The same Q is the ratio of reactance to resistance, and the danger and the radio front end in one number: microvolts at the aerial become millivolts at the capacitor.
Q multiplies voltages inside the circuit while the source sees only R; this is the tuned amplifier.
The magnification applies at resonance only; off-peak V_L and V_C differ and their difference is the source voltage.
A radio coil of 200 microhenry at 1 MHz with 5 ohm has Q = 251: a 10 microvolt aerial signal appears as 2.5 mV.

cards.title: Bandwidth and sharpness
items: The current falls to 1/root 2 of its peak where the net reactance equals R; solving near omega0 gives two half-power points omega0 plus or minus R/2L, a bandwidth R/L. The ratio of centre frequency to bandwidth is again Q: the same number measures magnification and narrowness.
The two definitions of Q are one identity; read the bandwidth straight off the resonance curve.
The half-power points are symmetric only for Q much greater than 1; at low Q the peak shifts slightly.
Bandwidth in hertz is R over 2 pi L: a 10 ohm, 10 mH coil is 160 Hz wide at any centre frequency.

cards.title: Q as an energy ratio
items: Stored half L I0 squared against dissipated half I0 squared R per cycle gives omega0 L/R: the third face of Q. A free oscillator rings about Q cycles before its amplitude falls appreciably; a coil of 10 mH with 2 ohm at 5 kHz has Q = 157 and rings a few hundred cycles.
Magnification, sharpness and ring time are the same number; know all three readings.
The energy ratio uses the PEAK stored energy convention; some texts use the mean and differ by a factor of 2.
Q = 100 means a hundred-cycle ring and a one per cent bandwidth: the settle time of the driven circuit.
Ring-down timing measures Q directly: count the cycles until the amplitude falls by a factor of e.

title: Power in AC circuits
subtitle: Sinusoidal steady state; linear loads with phase angle phi; RMS convention.
takeaway: Average power is V I cos phi; the power factor cos phi is what the customer pays for and the supply company hates.

cards.title: The average power
items: Instantaneous p = vi expands into a constant term and a double-frequency term; averaging kills the oscillation and leaves one half V0 I0 cos phi. Only the in-phase part of the current does work; the quadrature part shuttles energy back and forth.
Derive once from the product; then remember P = V I cos phi with RMS values, or one half V0 I0 with peaks.
Never mix one RMS and one peak value in the power formula; the factor of root 2 is the whole error.
Only the in-phase part of the current does work. Remember P = V I cos phi with RMS values or one half V0 I0 with peaks: never mix.

cards.title: The power triangle
items: Apparent power S in volt-amperes is the product of meter readings; real power P in watts is its projection on the current axis; reactive power Q_r in volt-amperes reactive is the perpendicular leg. Motors at 0.6 power factor draw 67 per cent more current than their watts suggest.
Three powers, one triangle; the billing meter reads watts but the wires carry volt-amperes.
The Q of the power triangle is NOT the quality factor of resonance; same letter, different meaning.
A 1 kW motor at 0.6 draws 1.67 kVA: 1.17 kVAR circulating through the supply.
The billing meter reads watts; the wires carry volt-amperes. A motor at 0.6 power factor draws 67 per cent more current than its watts suggest.

cards.title: Wattless current and correction
items: The 90-degree component of the current is wattless: it carries no average power but heats the wires and loads the generator. A parallel capacitor supplies the reactive volt-amperes locally, its current leading to cancel the motor current lagging; the supply then sees nearly unity power factor.
Correction is bookkeeping of reactive power done with a capacitor instead of the grid.
The correction capacitor is sized at the actual supply frequency; the formula fails on harmonics.
Correcting 0.6 to 0.95 cuts the line current by 37 per cent at equal real power.

cards.title: Energy over a cycle
items: In a full cycle the resistor absorbs PT; the inductor and capacitor each return exactly what they took, so the metered energy equals the real power times time. The instantaneous power oscillates at twice the source frequency for the reactive parts.
The energy ledger over one cycle separates the dissipating and shuttling components.
Half-cycle energy accounting misleads; the reactive parts integrate to zero only over whole cycles.
The capacitor stays cold; only the wires and generator carry the wattless current.
The instantaneous power dips negative twice per cycle in a purely reactive branch: energy sloshes back to the source.

title: Parallel AC circuits and the tank
subtitle: Linear branches sharing a voltage; sinusoidal steady state; admittance language.
takeaway: In parallel, admittances add; at resonance the line current is minimum and the tank circulates Q times it.

cards.title: Admittance
items: Parallel branches share voltage so their admittances add as series impedances do: conductance G = 1/R in phase, susceptances B = 1/X perpendicular. The line current is V times Y; the branch currents are the legs of the current triangle.
Switch to admittance before writing parallel equations; impedance arithmetic in parallel is painful.
Susceptance subtracts like reactance: capacitive and inductive branches cancel in the line.
I_{\rm line}=V Y,\qquad G=\frac1R,\ B_C=\omega C,\ B_L=\frac1{\omega L}
Convert each branch to G and B once; the network is then two numbers added component-wise.

cards.title: The tank circuit
items: At omega0 = 1/root(LC) the inductor and capacitor currents cancel in the supply line: the impedance is maximum and the line current minimum. Inside the LC loop a circulating current V omega0 C = Q times the line current flows back and forth, far larger than what the source supplies.
Anti-resonance: the opposite of the series case in every observable except the frequency.
The trap: two branch currents of 2 A each give line current zero at resonance, not 4 A.
The trap: two branch currents of 2 A each give line current zero at resonance, not 4 A. Inside the tank a circulating Q times the line current flows.

cards.title: Wave trap versus series
items: A parallel LC across a line rejects signals at omega0: the radio wave trap; a series LC in the line passes only omega0: the band-pass filter. Same frequency, opposite placement, opposite function.
Placement decides function: shunt to reject, series to select.
The rejection depth is set by Q; a low-Q tank is a shallow notch.
A 200 microhenry, 127 pF tank at 1 MHz with Q = 250 attenuates the line by 250 at resonance.
The IF transformer of a radio is this tank with taps: 455 kHz wide by design, not by accident. A detector diode after the tank needs only microvolts: selectivity first, gain second.

cards.title: Solving parallel networks
items: Add admittances of parallel branches, then convert back to Z for the phase. Mixed series-parallel networks go to complex impedance immediately; phasor diagrams alone get crowded fast. The worked R2 parallel C network gives Z = 25.9 ohm at -20 degrees for R1 = 10 in series.
One rule: series add Z, parallel add Y; mixed networks go complex.
Do not add branch currents as magnitudes; the phase offsets decide the line current.
20 ohm parallel 31.8 ohm capacitive reactance at 50 Hz: branch impedance 16.9 ohm at -32 degrees.
Series add Z, parallel add Y; mixed networks go complex immediately. Do not add branch currents as magnitudes.

title: Complex impedance and networks
subtitle: Linear circuits at one frequency; sinusoidal steady state; j-squared = -1 convention.
takeaway: Phasors are complex numbers: impedance arithmetic then does what phasor drawing cannot.

cards.title: The transform
items: Represent v = V0 sin(omega t + alpha) by V0 exp(j alpha); then d/dt becomes j omega and each element multiplies current by a complex impedance. Series impedances add and parallel combine by reciprocals: exactly like resistors, with phases carried in the argument.
The method converts phase bookkeeping into algebra; networks that defeat drawing fall to one line.
The physical quantity is the real part of the complex amplitude times exp(j omega t); a j surviving into a physical answer is an error.
\tilde V=\tilde Z\tilde I,\qquad Z=|\tilde Z|,\ \phi=\arg\tilde Z
Multiplying by j is a quarter-period phase lead: two j factors give the minus sign of the LC oscillator.

cards.title: Series LCR revisited
items: The complex impedance of the series circuit has magnitude Z and argument phi: the impedance triangle read as a complex number. Resonance is where the imaginary part vanishes; the phase is the arctan of imaginary over real.
Complex arithmetic reproduces the whole LCR sheet in one expression.
Keep the j convention consistent: j omega L for inductors, 1/(j omega C) = -j/(omega C) for capacitors.
The worked network R1 = 10 in series with 20 ohm parallel 100 microfarad at 50 Hz gives 24.3 - j 9.0 ohm.
The imaginary part vanishes at resonance. Keep the j convention consistent: j omega L for inductors and minus j over omega C for capacitors.

cards.title: Networks both ways
items: For the mixed network, rationalise the parallel part into real and imaginary parts; the real part dissipates and the imaginary part does not. Phasor drawing does the same in three lines of geometry: one line of algebra wins.
Read off Z and phi directly from the rationalised form; the physical split is real versus imaginary.
Power from complex amplitudes needs the conjugate: P = one half real part of V times conjugate I.
Power from complex amplitudes needs the conjugate: P = one half the real part of V times conjugate I. The rationalised form separates dissipation from storage.

cards.title: Limits of the method
items: Complex impedance is valid at one frequency; transients and harmonics need superposition of solutions at their own frequencies. The transient of the driven LCR is a decaying mode at the natural frequency plus the steady state at the drive.
A j that fails to cancel is the signal that two frequencies have been mixed.
Rectifier circuits draw harmonics; their correction needs each harmonic treated separately.
Switching transients die in about 2L/R seconds; after that the phasor solution is the circuit.
A surviving j in a physical answer flags a dropped conjugate or a mixed frequency.

title: Transformers and transmission
subtitle: Two coupled coils on a closed iron core; k near 1; sinusoidal steady state.
takeaway: The turns ratio sets voltage and current; the reflected impedance is the square of that ratio; the grid runs high voltage because losses scale as one over V squared.

cards.title: Flux linkage and voltage
items: The same flux links every turn of both windings: v = N dPhi/dt gives the voltage ratio equal to the turns ratio. The flux is set by the PRIMARY voltage: Phi0 = Vp0 / Np omega whatever the load draws. A transformer on DC makes no secondary EMF and the primary, seeing only its winding resistance, burns.
The load does not set the flux; the supply voltage does. The current follows the load.
Never connect a transformer to DC; steady flux means no induction and a shorted primary.

cards.title: Currents and power
